president-designate of the commission. - (it) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as in the previous debates, this fourth debate in parliament is taking place at a time when a particular crisis is shaking the international community. as was the case last spring in the balkans, the democratic will of the people of east timor is being flouted today, with the result that there is great suffering and serious threats to peace. until we are able to resolve this situation, i think we should have regrets. in the last few days i have used all the authority i have been given, even temporarily, to contact the indonesian authorities. i have a telephone conversation with president habibie at 2 p.m. today and i think we should put as much pressure as possible, make every effort to put an end to this situation. (applause) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the time has come for the vote on the new commission. i have explained to you on several occasions why i believe that our programme is the right one to lead the european commission for the next five years. you got to know its members, both through the written answers they gave to your questionnaires and through the hearings you had with each of them. i want to pay tribute to the dignity and professionalism that characterized these hearings. i hope that your vote tomorrow will mark a new beginning in the relations between our two institutions because now - if the commission is approved - it is time, after so many months, to get to work. together we must put europe at the service of the citizens. we must restore citizens' confidence in europe and in a european vision that puts their needs first. i want our two institutions and the council - the triangle that governs the european union - to work together, serving the european citizens truly and effectively. i am determined to transform the commission into a modern and efficient administration which has learned from recent experience and put its house in order. the reform process already under way in the commission is only at its beginning. in february 2000, mr kinnock, who is here with me, will present a comprehensive reform programme which will take careful account of the second report of the committee of independent experts. it goes without saying that we will consult and inform the european parliament about the progress made in this area. the commission intends to become much more open. the time for transparency has come. i want europe to be no longer done behind closed doors and to be exposed to the full scrutiny of the public. i want the public to be able to look over my shoulder and see that the commission is really dealing with the issues that concern them most. i mean, i'm gonna keep going the way i started. wherever possible, the new commission will seek to match european best practice. there are many examples for us to follow, and we will try to follow the best of them. for example, i am considering keeping my correspondence in a public register so that it can be examined at will, as is done in the more open countries of europe. and the new commission will make much greater efforts to communicate properly with the citizens of europe, giving them free access to information. the democratic health of the european union and the obligation to be accountable to all citizens require transparency. i would now like to come to what this new commission will do, if it is given the mandate, after having spoken of the method. i would also like to refer to the programmes which have already been discussed in previous speeches in this parliament and which are still valid. in january, as agreed, the commission will present the policies it proposes to pursue over the next five years, and this presentation will be closely followed by the presentation of the work programme for the year 2000. it is also essential that we have a big policy debate at the beginning of each year. i know you share my opinion on this. i know that you share my choice and that is why in future i intend to present an annual political and economic report on the state of the european union. this report will summarise the information currently contained in a series of - sometimes uncoordinated - commission studies, and this should be a unifying element in our policy-making process. i hope that together we can organise the political debate and the process of mutual consultation in a much more coherent way than before. today i would like to give you a very quick overview of three fundamental challenges we are facing: the enlargement of the european union and how it affects our relations with our neighbours. reform of the institutions of the european union and preparation for the next intergovernmental conference. strengthening economic growth, job creation and sustainable development. we are the heirs of a bold and visionary project and when we plan for the future we must remember all that we have already achieved. we have created a customs union and a single market based on the free movement of goods, services, capital and people. we have built an economic and monetary union with a single currency. we have laid the foundations for a political union with common institutions and a strong european parliament elected by universal suffrage. what we must now build is a union of hearts and minds, based on a shared sense of a community of destiny, on a consciousness of a common european citizenship. we're from different countries. we speak different languages. we have different historical and cultural traditions and we must preserve these diversities. but today we are looking for a shared identity - a new european soul. the vision of the founding fathers fifty years ago was to create a community based on peace, stability and prosperity. this european ideal is as important to citizens today as it was then. as i stand before you today, peace, stability and prosperity are still our great common goal. this is why enlargement of the european union is both a difficult and an extraordinary challenge. our attitude to enlargement is a mirror reflecting our deep political convictions. can we be satisfied with having achieved peace, stability and prosperity only for ourselves, the 15 member states? i do not think so, and the balkan episode proves that it is not possible. the question is therefore: will we have the courage, the vision and the ambition to offer real prospects of peace, stability and prosperity to an enlarged union, to those outside and those who will not be inside the union, to the european countries close to us? this century has seen devastating conflicts that have divided our continent. we, the citizens of the european union, have turned our backs on them and we must help our neighbours to walk in the same direction. i'm not saying it's going to be easy. it requires a comprehensive strategy defining how, over the next 25 years, we will expand the european union from 15 to 20, 25 or even 30 member states. this process will require many sacrifices, many changes and transformations between us and within us. this strategy must take account of three things. firstly, the fact that enlargement will inevitably take place in several stages: some countries will join before others. secondly, the specific needs of those countries which will have to wait longer before joining. thirdly, how will this enlargement process affect our other neighbours whose accession is not on the agenda but with whom we wish to have close and constructive relations, which are also necessary for peace and prosperity? i would like to make very clear on the first point: we must have a political vision, not a technocratic one. we must define a genuine enlargement strategy which brings together, beyond accession, the european nations into a single family. this means, first of all, that we must seriously consider in helsinki the possibility of defining the date of accession for the countries which are best prepared, even if this means that they will have to be given long transitional periods to solve their political, social and economic problems. this also has implications for the next intergovernmental conference, to which i shall return in a moment. then there is the fundamental question of the impact of enlargement on our common policies. the more we enlarge, the more difficult it will become to define what really needs to be dealt with at european level and what needs to be dealt with at a lower level. we really must implement subsidiarity, which is a basic principle of europe. i do not claim to be able to answer that today, but we must have the courage to face this problem seriously and honestly. the second point is that we must be creative and resourceful in responding to the needs of those countries for whom membership is a longer-term prospect. i am thinking of closer cooperation with these countries, perhaps by allowing them 'virtual membership' - excuse the expression but it is difficult to find a better one, it is a didactic expression anyway - in certain areas as a prelude to real membership which would take place much later. they could, for example, be offered the fullest possible participation in economic and monetary union, new forms of security cooperation and new forms of relations, adapted to their needs, with the european institutions, in which they would be consulted or would have observer status, in an empirical and specific way. the situation in the balkans deserves our particular attention. the prospect of these countries joining the european union is not imminent, but we must use it to put them on the path to peaceful coexistence and closer interregional partnership. i say it clearly: the peoples of these countries must settle their conflicts themselves before they can join the european union. they must not think that they can bring it into the union and have it dealt with by us, but we must help them to solve it. however, they are undeniably in need of our help, and i would like to stress the special responsibility of the european commission in the huge and necessary reconstruction effort. our citizens expect the european union to take the moral and political lead, particularly in a region that is right on our doorstep. we can't afford to let them down. i am also concerned that the debate on the future of the balkans has already lost its force and dramatic character in a few weeks, as if we were somehow trying to put it on the back burner. the third element of the strategy must be a clear and comprehensive approach to our closest neighbours, whose contribution to the peace and stability of enlarged europe is vital. such a strategy will only succeed if it is inclusive. we all - whether the european union, the candidate countries or our neighbours in the enlarged europe - must work together to forge our common destiny: a wider european space, offering peace, stability and european prosperity. we must create a new european order. this should include 'strategic partnerships' with russia and ukraine, adapted to the geopolitical dimension of these countries. this new strategy should also include a 'partnership of cultures' - a term i am tempted to suggest for a new, more ambitious, much more ambitious commitment to the mediterranean, where we europeans are determined to promote a new form of exemplary collaboration between the peoples of the three religions of jerusalem, to oppose a resolute 'no' to the struggle between civilizations. i must say a word about the importance of our strategic relations with the united states. we need a stronger transatlantic partnership, capable of genuine shared leadership. our first opportunity to do so will be the launch of the ambitious millennium round in seattle, which is designed to further advance all wto members. let us be farsighted and smart and seize this opportunity, opening a new chapter in global trade relations. let me now turn to the second challenge that we face in the immediate future. this is the next intergovernmental conference (igc). we have always known that enlargement would raise profound questions about the way in which the institutions function. however, the recent crisis in the commission and the low turnout in the 1999 european elections have shown that a truly ambitious reform of the european institutions is now imperative. the amsterdam treaty - which has been positive in some respects - has not been up to the task of meeting the major institutional issues. a formula of proceeding in stages, through a series of intergovernmental conferences without deadlines, seems to me particularly unattractive. it would put europe in a state of perpetual constitutional reform which would be incomprehensible to our citizens and to our neighbours. it would also be a huge waste of much needed energy elsewhere, such as in the construction of new policies. we cannot therefore afford to settle for a minimalist reform which does not equip us for energetic and effective decision-making. as you know, i have asked mr dehaene, mr von weizsäcker and lord simon to draw up a report on which the commission will base its own position on the questions to be addressed by the igc. this report will be submitted to you and i hope that we will have a constructive debate in the period immediately preceding helsinki. we must express our views loud and clear because the coming months will be of crucial importance in determining whether we enter a new era strong and firmly armed or weak and withdrawn. however, europe is not just a matter of institutions; it is also a matter of citizens. for europe to prosper, europeans must have jobs and we must put europe back to work. to create jobs, you need a healthy economy. the third major challenge we face is how to ensure ecologically and economically sustainable growth that creates new jobs. after a difficult period, europe is now experiencing an economic recovery. growth is back, although it's not yet evenly distributed, but the signs of growth are good. the sometimes painful process of convergence towards economic and monetary union - coupled with the responsible attitude of the economic and social partners towards wage increases - has finally created the macroeconomic conditions for healthy growth. the introduction of the euro has consolidated this trend. the stability programmes of the member states will further develop this. that's great news. but it also places a very heavy responsibility on us. the economic recovery offers us a great opportunity to make structural adjustments at lower cost. modernizing the european economy today means more european jobs for tomorrow. we cannot afford to miss this opportunity, as we have too often done in the past. we must therefore take advantage of the more favourable prospects for the coming years to ensure that growth remains strong for as long as possible, creates the jobs we need and is accompanied by a renewed and genuine commitment to sustainable development. we must also tackle the long-term problems arising from the new demographic trends - which are one of the major problems facing europe and which we will have to consider together - and their impact on the fabric of our societies. in the final analysis, this means that both productivity per worker and the number of participants in the labour force must be increased. if we succeed in doing so, we will have a real opportunity to build a just and sustainable society. the single market has given new vitality to our economies and is contributing to the current recovery. however, we must continue to restructure this single market and promote liberalisation to further stimulate competition in the goods sector and, in particular, in the services sector. this will help us to maximise the job creation potential of growth and, in the longer term, support higher growth in our production capacity. this is not the time to go into the details of the structural reforms needed, which have already been described in many commission reports. we must now begin to implement them. i would like to mention one particular challenge among those we are facing, however, which is to be added to the proposals already made at other meetings we have held on health, sport and other issues. this challenge is about information technologies which are transforming the way we live and work and the way businesses operate. they enable individuals and businesses to achieve things that were unthinkable just a few years ago. the impressive performance of the us economy is largely explained by the enthusiasm with which the us has embraced information technology. i am concerned that european countries seem reluctant to exploit the full potential of these technologies. modern economies are increasingly knowledge-based and this is one area where we have a competitive advantage globally. encouraging the use and development of information technologies will therefore be a priority for the new commission. i propose that we launch an initiative in this area at the helsinki summit. it will be an ambitious initiative, which will have to appeal to all young people in europe. finally, we must take advantage of the economic recovery and stronger growth to adapt our social systems to current demographic trends. we can no longer ignore the problems or postpone decisions: the pensioners of the year 2050 are already among us! a highly developed social system is one of the distinguishing features of our european societies and we must preserve it. but we owe it to our children to adapt it so that it offers them credible promises as close as possible to those it has offered to our generation. the commission has recently proposed an ambitious strategy for closer european cooperation in this area and i will attach particular importance to this. in all these difficult tasks, the european union has a key role to play. firstly, because it is more effective to seek to solve long-term problems through concerted european strategies - such as the european employment process - than by acting at the purely national or local level, even if this is necessary. secondly, because action at european level often makes it easier to avoid the deadlocks that result from the more immediate pressures of national political calendars. so we have a little bit more of a backlog of these problems and we have to look at them in a broader context. we have the tools to do that. for example, following the luxembourg summit, strong progress has been made in developing a genuine european employment strategy in which the combination of guidelines, peer reviews and recommendations finally provides a powerful incentive for change. we must therefore continue this process, deepening cooperation at european level so that we can focus all our attention and all our action on the major structural reforms needed to revitalise our economy. that is possible today. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, you are the democratically elected representatives of the citizens of europe. you represent the various european political families in all their diversity and complexity. i hope you will give your full support to the new commission in your vote tomorrow. i am sticking to the political commitments i made at the conference of presidents last week, which must now be incorporated into a new framework agreement governing our future work. let's move on. let us encourage a new spirit of cooperation between our institutions, a new balance, based not only on mutual respect but also on deep cooperation. a new partnership for the benefit of the european citizens. a new commission a new european parliament is needed. a fresh start. all the council's fine words do not change the fact that for 90% of the legal documents promulgated, the council itself acts. and how does it work? the 15 executives go to brussels, act like a legislative body, then return to their respective capitals, once again applying the laws enacted by the council itself. this means that, by their current mode of operation, the executive is increasingly excluding national parliaments - this is evident in the case of europol and in the establishment of the europol convention - and is not transferring the legislative function to the european parliament. in this context of parliamentary inadequacy, it is not possible to develop in a democratic way an area of security, freedom and justice which represents the development of a structure which takes into account the requirements of protection of the individual and which includes the possibility of interfering in the private sphere. the european parliament must therefore appeal to the council and the commission. it is precisely in the areas in which you have already decided - in a way that i think is too cowardly - to give the european parliament the same legislative rights that you must ensure that we in tampere have the same legislative rights by the next intergovernmental conference if you want to build a democratic area of security, freedom and justice. otherwise you risk seeing citizens moving further away from the european union.

company. it is largely state-owned. the question of land ownership is not clarified either. all these are the main tasks which the agency will have to carry out and this can only be done on the spot! commission - mr president, i must confess that as i listened to the debates in a very large format this afternoon, i was reminded of the maxim that if the situation depresses you in domestic affairs, it will make you despair in international affairs. none of us can afford to be so pessimistic and that is why voices have been raised in this democratic chamber to express deep concern and call for action. i welcome that very sincerely. this shows that there are better and more interesting things to do than to give in to despair, as representatives and political activists as well as the general public may sometimes be tempted to do. may i begin with the debate on kosovo and the various tragedies that are affecting this sad part of the world? the commission fully shares the concerns expressed in the motions for resolutions tabled in the house. these concerns concern the continuing ethnic violence in kosovo as well as the previous disappearances and imprisonments. we naturally join with members of this parliament in strongly condemning violence, irrespective of the ethnic group responsible or the victim, and we actively support the efforts of minuk, kfor and the osce to restore public order in kosovo. the commission shares the deep concern of this house for the fate of the many civilians who have not yet been found. we are therefore directly involved in the efforts to find out which of the missing persons are still in serbian prisons, which were killed during the war and under what circumstances. the union is therefore cooperating with the forensic investigations into the allegations of war crimes and, earlier this week, the general affairs council expressed its concern that the question of the thousands of missing - the vast majority of whom are kosovo albanians - was still unresolved. finally, the commission has repeatedly condemned the clear failure of the authorities of the federal republic of yugoslavia, serbia, to respect the standards accepted by the international community in the field of humanity and minority rights. the disregard for international obligations thus manifested is one of the main obstacles to the improvement of relations between the former yugoslav republic and the european union and also an obstacle to the return of the former republic to the international community. there is a strong chance that this obstacle will remain as long as the serbian authorities continue with their current policy. i now turn to the resolution on the situation in burma. the assembly is aware that the commission sincerely deplores the continuing human rights violations by the burmese military authorities, including the oppression of ethnic minorities, the persecution of aung san suu kyi and other members of the nld, the denial of basic trade union rights and the use of forced labour, the prohibition of free opposition, the incalculable number of arbitrary arrests and a state of continuing violence. we also share the concerns expressed about the treatment of european union citizens who have been arrested for openly engaging in pro-democracy activities in burma. in april this year, the european union's common position reinforced the political decision of october 1998, extending it to transit visas and banning tourist visits by people linked to the burmese authorities. the commission was in favour of this initiative; it supports the democratic movement and the refugees in burma, including, of course, financial aid to the brussels office. the council is currently reviewing the common position and, as the honourable members pointed out during the debate, its extension should be decided before 29 october. the commission has made it clear that although burma has become a member of asean, the european union cannot accept burma's participation in the ec-asean agreement. we take every opportunity to put pressure on our asian partners to urge the burmese government to engage in a broad dialogue with the opposition, led by aung san suu kyi, and ethnic minorities and to make a radical change in policy to respect human rights. you are aware that aung san suu kyi recently renewed her call for the strengthening of international economic sanctions against burma, including unilateral sanctions, as long as the current regime controls the country she loves. the commission took part in the recent visit of the european troika to rangoon, which was intended to lay the first foundations for a political dialogue with burma, as provided for in the council conclusions of 26 april. the purpose of the political dialogue is to explain the common position of the european union on the treatment of human rights and the absence of the rule of law and democracy in burma and to help create the conditions for a political dialogue between the spdc, the ruling military junta, on the one hand, and the democratic opposition and representatives of ethnic minorities, on the other. the european commission intends to keep up the pressure on the spdc, the former slorc. in the meantime, the international situation continues to deteriorate and the repeated appeals of the international community to the burmese authorities to take initiatives to promote democracy, human rights and national reconciliation are not receiving much response. the commission therefore remains in favour of renewing the common position next month and of strict application of the pressure and sanctions that follow. i now turn to iran, which is again the subject of our attention following the resolutions submitted to this house. you are aware that the commission shares with this house its deep concern about the human rights situation in iran. the representatives of the european union are constantly returning to the issues directly related to human rights in the context of our comprehensive dialogue with iran. although the commission has no bilateral contractual relationship with iran, nor any representation in that country, it is associated with the approach of the eu troika. the treatment of members of religious minorities in iran, particularly the baha'is, was raised by the troika in meetings with the iranian government in december last year and may this year. we will keep up the pressure on this. as regards the specific points relating to the human rights violations raised by mr zimeray and mr morillon and ms malmström, i would say that the finnish presidency is busy working out, following the death sentences of four students, a policy of the union troika which echoes the views expressed by this parliament. the commission is also concerned about the trial of 13 jews from chiraz on charges of espionage. the union has taken several steps in this respect, both through the troika and bilaterally. it is clear that the recent developments in iran reflect the power struggle between moderate reformists and hardline conservatives within the country. the conservatives' efforts to take back the initiative and undermine the government should be seen as a prelude to the general elections scheduled for february. in the meantime, the commission considers that, especially in the run-up to the elections, the policy of cautious openness towards iran must be continued through a broad dialogue, in order to encourage the khatami government and the reformists, many of whom are showing considerable courage in working for change in extremely difficult and dangerous conditions. i now turn to the problem of togo. the assembly is aware that in 1992 the european community suspended its development cooperation with togo. despite some changes since then, i regret to say that the conditions for the resumption of development cooperation and the full normalisation of relations with togo - respect for democratic principles, the rule of law and human rights - are not yet sufficiently met. however, some progress towards political reconciliation has been made thanks to the lomé framework agreement concluded between the government and the opposition in july this year. this progress has been made possible by the european union observers, as mr watson has pointed out. the union therefore intends to support the continued efforts of these observers, as well as projects related to the full restoration of the rule of law and respect for human rights. the commission welcomes the will expressed by the government and the opposition to make progress on the framework agreement, but further substantial progress - for example the successful holding of early parliamentary elections next year - is required before we can consider resuming regular cooperation. the commission shares the specific concerns about the human rights situation in togo as expressed in the resolutions submitted to this house. it is very worrying that the human rights violations recently reported by amnesty international have been largely confirmed by other sources. however, some of the most serious accusations of mass killings have not yet been verified. the commission therefore considers that the investigations should be continued. the assembly should know that wherever problems arise in relation to human rights, the united nations system provides a whole range of monitoring mechanisms to promote the improvement of the situation. the commission believes that such mechanisms should be considered in the case of togo. it would seem that they are quite justified. commission - mr president, let me once again express the commission's thanks to the members for the way in which they have brought this very important matter to the attention of the house this afternoon. the commission considers that the european union, together with the rest of the international community, must take decisive initiatives to contain the repercussions of the crisis in the great lakes countries, a crisis which, as the honourable members have pointed out, threatens in many ways the stability and security of the whole of africa. the european union's policy is therefore based on the need to deal with the repercussions of the great lakes conflict in its threefold dimension: regional, with the need not to lose sight of the interests of neighbouring countries; national, with the need to take into account the interests of the government, rebel groups and the democratic opposition; and finally, local, with clashes between communities, generated by ethnic rivalries and strong social pressures. in this context, the union is making significant efforts to mediate and promote dialogue at the various levels of the conflict, and the commission is ready to contribute to the success of the lusaka ceasefire agreement in the following areas. firstly, in terms of political support, the european union intends to continue and encourage the efforts already undertaken by our special representative for the great lakes region to achieve sufficient intensity of dialogue between the different factions involved in the conflict in the democratic republic of congo. the union is determined to continue to promote and finance mediation efforts, in particular those of the zambian president, who was the first to make the lusaka agreement possible. this action is necessary to try to prevent signatories from reneging on their commitment to comply with their obligations. the lusaka agreement provides for a national debate in the drc to reconcile the various political forces in the drc and to shape a new political landscape in the drc. the commission is also prepared to finance mediation efforts to bring about this national debate. secondly, among the efforts we are committed to provide is support for peacekeeping operations by the united nations and the organization of african unity. several member states are contributing to the team of 90 un military observers in the region's capitals and between the rebel groups' military commands to monitor the implementation of the lusaka agreement. these actions should also support the joint military commission responsible for organising the deployment of a peacekeeping or peace-keeping force. the un security council has yet to decide on the nature of such a force. the union will then be able to decide what support to give and how. thirdly, as regards economic and development support, the commission could and should reactivate its commitments under the lomé convention provided that the following two conditions are met: first, an improvement in the security situation in the drc and, second, the conclusion of the national debate in a stable political landscape which respects the main provisions of the lomé convention. the commission's support for the reconstruction and development effort would then focus on the following points: first, the establishment of the rule of law and the democratization of national institutions; second, the demobilization and socioeconomic reintegration of the belligerents; thirdly, restoration of the environment, especially in the provinces of kivu and eastern kivu; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject. of course, i am also sensitive to the call, among others, by mrs maes for a strict halt to arms trafficking of all kinds, which continues to fuel conflicts in the region and which often originates from here, from the european union. finally, it is clear that humanitarian aid is a permanent necessity and the european community humanitarian office, echo, has made some €55.5 million available this year. we will continue our efforts to support a lasting stability. it is also natural that we will continue to ensure that parliament is fully informed, because we greatly appreciate its commitment to our common objectives of stability and lasting peace in this sorely tried region. commission. - (it) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, in recent years, and especially in recent months, an uninterrupted series of food scandals has traumatized the european citizens whom you represent. today, as in the past, citizens no longer trust what they put on their plates, and they no longer trust governments or even scientists to guarantee that food products are truly natural. our task today is to do everything we can to ensure that this loss of consumer confidence does not happen again. this problem concerns us personally, you and me, as it does every european consumer. so we have a responsibility to protect the health of our fellow citizens. we therefore have a duty to take decisive action quickly, as our citizens want. food safety is an integral part of health protection. it is therefore a crucial problem, also because of its cultural dimension, which we must not neglect. the problem of food is part of the european lifestyle and identity. that is why food safety has become a top priority for the commission, and i am delighted that this discussion on public health and food safety is the first sector-specific discussion of my mandate. in terms of hygiene and safety, we must anticipate action, to use a sporting metaphor, rather than limit ourselves to extinguishing fires, as we have done so far; we have to smother them in the egg, anticipate their formation. to achieve this, an effective and credible food security system needs to be established. as a consumer, i must know exactly what is in a food product, a package, a can, and i have a right to know because this right is, among other things, guaranteed by the amsterdam treaty. the labels do not always give me complete information and i am not always aware of the nutritional and health implications of my choice. i often don't understand the environmental and ethical implications of the manufacturing process. suppose the newspapers report a food scandal. as a consumer, i cannot understand whether there is a real reason for alarm or whether this is just a journalistic invention. if i look on the internet, a lot of information is not understandable. in short, i do not know whether the information is credible or whether it has been manipulated for political and economic purposes. these are just some of the aspects of consumer policy which we need to look at. citizens need to know exactly what they are eating. allowing consumers access to a community early warning system could be a step forward, ensuring that this system covers both agricultural products and animal feed. this would allow the dissemination of a system which would allow us to avoid too counterproductive alerts and simply shout "fire! fire!" however, too many recent warnings have proved to be justified. we must therefore strengthen our food inspection system. the whole production chain, from upstream to downstream, must be carefully and rigorously controlled at each stage and in each member state. in the single market, all citizens have the right to equal protection. we therefore need to update the legislation on which the food inspection system is based. the commission presented a green paper in 1997 which will have to be followed by adequate and substantive provisions to refine and update our food legislation. for example, when it comes to food products and processed foods, more than 100 basic guidelines are now in force. we need one single set of rules. food legislation will also have to cover the whole food chain, from farmers to consumers and from animal feed production, which has been one of the most sensitive points in recent months. this legislation will have to be flexible in order to allow it to be adapted to the evolution of scientific knowledge and new production techniques. it should be based on sound and up-to-date scientific information and advice. at present the commission is consulting high-level scientists whose opinions are transparent and whose interests are publicly stated. but it is absolutely essential that we regain the confidence of the citizens in our food choices. scientists must be independent of any obscure political pressure. the establishment of an independent european food agency could help us achieve this. many member states have already started this process and have set up independent food safety authorities. a european food agency could, for example, be modelled on the emea, the european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products. this agency has no decision-making power but it carries out highly technical work with great speed and efficiency. if a drug causes a problem, this agency is able to determine the cause within hours. but in the case of a food alert, this can take weeks and weeks. the agency could also be modelled on the us federal food and drug administration, which has considerable initiative and decision-making powers. such a body would enable rapid intervention in food security in a politically independent manner. the problem, of course, is how to ensure that decisions are taken democratically. and that is why it is so important that this debate be held before parliament. that is why we are here today, because there is no doubt that we are faced with a choice in which the problem of democracy is extremely important. i am not sure that this agency can be set up with the guarantees that some people are calling for under the treaty. here too we must look deeper into the problem. my choice is not yet made, it's a choice we must make together. but let us remember that consumers need clear, precise but also strong choices and that there is no room for uncertainty, because uncertainty has been too much in all these years. i would add, moreover, that security is becoming an international value, as has been demonstrated by the controversies with the united states and other countries. the world trade organisation is the appropriate framework for resolving these disputes and, in the context of the millennium round, the european union will push for credible international food safety standards, with the participation of consumer representatives. we will also have to shed light on how the precautionary principle has been applied in food safety. this is another pillar. the idea behind the precautionary principle is very simple: temporary safety measures should be taken when scientific information is incomplete and safety is in doubt. the problem, however, is that scientific information is always incomplete because the limits of our knowledge are constantly changing. the precautionary principle therefore raises questions: what level of health concern should be reached? who has to make a value judgment before introducing trade restrictive measures on the basis of the precautionary principle? what scientific knowledge must we have before we have to abandon these measures? we need to clarify these various points and a parliamentary debate is appropriate. i would like to stress that consumer health protection will be at the heart of the trade negotiations initiated by the european union. we are categorically opposed to the community signing international agreements which we believe endanger the health of european citizens, even though this may be highly controversial. i would also like to emphasize that the union's food policy must have food safety as its fundamental objective and that it should be at the service of consumers and their health. health is therefore a priority. i am convinced that a strict food safety policy also serves the interests of european farmers and the european processing industry: agricultural and processing companies must be at the forefront of producing high quality food. here, public trust is essential. what initiatives does the commission intend to take? we want to avoid disorderly reactions leading to disorderly measures. we must be cautious, concerned and determined. food security is an area in which we must proceed very cautiously, not in haste but with a certain degree of speed. before the end of the year we will therefore be presenting to the council and parliament a white paper on food safety and a communication on the precautionary principle which requires further study. the white paper will contain an action plan for food security, accompanied by a precise timetable of initiatives for the next three years, including options for the european food agency. we are aiming at a thorough reform of food legislation and to this end all the commission's proposals will be presented by the end of the year 2000. on this basis, we intend to have an updated organic set of rules by the year 2002, as it will take some time to develop. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the foodstuffs are not contaminated. we must, however, ensure that consumer representatives are involved in this decision-making process in a much more intensive way. the task of educating and guiding the public is in fact the responsibility of consumer representatives. there are very important issues involved, issues that may even cause emotional reactions. clearly, though, to be fruitful, a discussion must not take place in an atmosphere of emotional dominance. i therefore sincerely hope that our debate will be distinguished not by the tensions it will generate but by the clarity it will succeed in bringing. we must feel safe ourselves and we must share that security with the citizens. the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, the altener programme is part of the multiannual action programme in the field of energy for the period 1998-2002 and deals with the essential chapter on alternative renewable energies. the commission's proposal dates from november 1997. as early as march 1999, the former parliament had delivered its opinion at first reading following the report by our former colleague, mr carlos robles piquer. with the entry into force of the amsterdam treaty, the legal basis has changed: the multiannual energy programme is now subject to the co-decision procedure. following this change in the legal basis, the european commission proceeded, immediately after the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam on 21 may 1999, to the amendment and fundamental revision of its proposal on the basis of the decisions taken by parliament on 11 march 1999. the council adopted the common position on 28 june. parliament can now see that both the commission and the council have largely taken up its proposals and i would therefore like to thank them for this constructive collaboration as rapporteur for the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy. the second reading will now be the time for parliament to consider whether the common position still requires improvements. the industry committee issued a unanimous recommendation in this regard on 22 september. the parliament and the commission have a common objective of increasing the share of renewable energy in the community's gross energy consumption to 12% by 2010. that's about twice the current rate. it is an ambitious goal that requires enormous efforts. the compromises which have now been found are only a step in that direction. parliament considered that it was essential that member states in particular should redouble their efforts. the funds allocated to the altener programme are so modest that they will not allow this ambitious objective to be achieved. our amendments - there are nine in all - require member states to make a voluntary commitment to promote renewable energy. a charter should address the fact that no chapter of the treaty on european union is specifically devoted to energy policy. in addition, in article 1 (1), parliament expresses its willingness to implement the campaign for renewable energy sources already called for in the 1997 white paper and to create new instruments and mechanisms to promote the accelerated and coordinated market penetration of all sustainable energy technologies. moreover, the central and eastern european states and, as the liberal group has rightly requested, the mediterranean states must play a significant role in this implementation. parliament would like to insert in article 5 of the altener programme a remark on the new procedure for the exercise of implementing powers in order to improve the involvement of the european parliament. we are convinced that part iv of the multiannual action programme on energy cannot meet all the requirements. i would like to remind you of the second report we have today, mrs ahern's report on energy efficiency. however, i would also point out that the introduction of alternative energy sources confronts us with two important issues: hydropower and wind energy, whose coverage is proportionately as large as the others (e.g. solar energy or the use of biomass), must be encouraged in an extremely intensive way. i am delighted and pleased that you now have responsibility for this important subject, commissioner, because as a former spanish minister of agriculture you know that in agricultural policy it is probably more appropriate to reduce surpluses than to devote useful land to the energy exploitation of biomass. i know, however, that there is still relatively great resistance in this area, and that it comes from industry but also from agricultural policy, but we should nevertheless join our efforts in order to link agricultural policy and energy policy in the field of renewable energies. i would like to congratulate you on the good cooperation we have had and i hope that this report will receive a majority in this parliament.

the european union is closely monitoring the democratic development of its partner. the human rights situation in turkey, including the rights of minorities, is seriously flawed. unfortunately, we hear too often about restrictions on freedom of expression, for example, which are not in line with our european values. we have, however, noted with satisfaction the recent steps taken by the turkish government to implement democratic reforms and improve the human rights situation. we also want to encourage turkey to continue on the path of reform. the osce conference in istanbul on 18 and 19 november will be an important opportunity for turkey to demonstrate its commitment to promoting universally accepted civil liberties. the european union is opposed to the death penalty everywhere and in all cases. the general abolition of the death penalty worldwide is a common objective of the european union. turkish legislation still allows for the death penalty and the execution of this penalty. however, no executions have been carried out in the country since 1984. we want turkey to suspend the execution of the death sentences already handed down, including that of mr öcalan, the leader of the pkk. we expect turkey to abolish the death penalty completely from its legislation and to continue its moratorium in the meantime. we also recall that the suspension of the death penalty is one of the common values of the european union, to which turkey has declared its wish to join. an encouraging development has recently begun to emerge in relations between turkey and greece. we greatly appreciate greece's contribution to this development and we regard the dialogue between the two countries as extremely positive. it was touching to see the genuine expressions of sympathy and solidarity after the earthquakes in turkey and greece. we hope that the positive climate which has developed in recent times can be a step towards a more lasting improvement in relations between the two countries. increased cooperation increases trust, which in turn contributes to strengthening stability in the western mediterranean and in europe as a whole. it's in our mutual interest. although the dialogue i mentioned earlier is optimistic, there are still some difficult questions. the european union and the presidency fully support the efforts of the un to find a lasting and just solution to the situation in cyprus. we hope that progress will be made in solving this problem, which has lasted for too long, as early as this autumn. we are confident that turkey will do its part to help find a fair solution. on a visit to turkey two weeks ago, i heard that the damage caused by the august earthquake was the worst in europe since the second world war. turkey cannot cope with the demanding task of reconstruction on its own. there is no precise data yet on the cost of repairing the damage, with estimates ranging from us$3 billion to us$6.5 billion. the earthquake left 400,000 homeless, who are currently living in tent cities. with the arrival of winter, they will no longer be able to live in such conditions. the european union wishes to help turkey in its immense reconstruction work. we are confident of constructive cooperation from the european parliament in this important area as well. during its presidency, finland will do all it can to deepen turkey's integration into european structures. the exchange of letters between the previous presidency and the turkish prime minister, mr ecevit, provides a good basis for the presidency's efforts. in his letter, mr ecevit confirmed that turkey's accession efforts would be based on the copenhagen criteria. the member states of the european union are unanimous in their view of the importance of turkey as a cooperation partner and the need for closer cooperation. the european union and the member states in particular have stressed this on many occasions. only a few days ago, prime minister simitis and german chancellor schröder said that the european union would make a serious effort to achieve a positive result at the forthcoming helsinki summit. the key issue is the confirmation of turkey's candidate status. to achieve this, the european union as well as turkey will have to work actively and show goodwill. we are firmly convinced that bringing turkey closer to the european union is the best way to support the implementation of democratic reforms in the country. the isolationist approach in this case is not conducive to turkey's objectives, nor to those of the european union. in this work we absolutely need the support of the european parliament for concrete measures and general support for the development and rapprochement of relations between the european union and turkey.
the commission is particularly pleased that the european parliament is dealing with the subject of turkey today, shortly after the start of its work, in a detailed debate, because this is one of the most important political and strategic questions we have to solve in europe at the present time. today's discussions take place at a time when relations between the european union and turkey have the opportunity to take a new direction: exactly two months before the european council meeting in helsinki, which is expected to take important decisions on the whole enlargement process and, above all, on turkey. the council representative has just given us a political analysis of the present situation, which the commission can wholeheartedly endorse. i would like to make a few additional comments on this from the commission's point of view. since the european council meeting in luxembourg in december 1997, relations between the european union and turkey have deteriorated for reasons that are well known. as you are aware, turkey did not consider the european council's finding that it was eligible for membership to be sufficient. shortly after the european council in december 1997, the commission adopted the famous european strategy for preparing turkey for membership in all important areas. this european strategy was developed as a specific, tailor-made strategy for rapprochement, with the aim of extending and deepening the existing customs union. the commission's proposals received political backing at the cardiff summit in june 1998. since cardiff, several meetings have taken place to implement specific aspects of this strategy but the lack of appropriate funding has so far prevented any substantial progress, although i must add that the overall picture is not as bleak as it is sometimes presented. the customs union has been improved in some areas and exploratory talks on the possibility of a free trade agreement in the services sector have made good progress. commission experts have been to turkey to improve our general knowledge of turkish legislation in all the relevant areas. as regards financing, i would point out that by the end of the year turkey will receive eur 375 million under the meda i financing programme. we must, however, make further efforts to respect the agreements reached with turkey. the commission would like to encourage parliament to give its opinion as soon as possible on the draft regulations which are to support the european strategy. without this financial support, the credibility of the european strategy is threatened. this credibility is essential, however, and it is also essential to convince the turkish side that it must make an active contribution to the implementation of this strategy. if we really want to help turkey in its preparation for membership, as the luxembourg european council wanted when it initiated this european strategy, we must also show that we will make a significant contribution to achieving this objective. there is no doubt that the european parliament has a key role to play in this process. i should like to say how pleased i am that the commission reacted so quickly after the terrible earthquake which struck turkey on 17 august. the decision to release €30 million in emergency reconstruction aid was made possible by the quick response of the budgetary authorities. in addition, the european investment bank will provide medium-term loans of up to eur 600 million for reconstruction and macrofinancial assistance of up to eur 200 million to ensure that ongoing reforms are in line with the international monetary fund. but we have to look ahead. as has already been said, the european council in helsinki will again consider the question of the european union's relations with turkey. in this respect, i would like to make it very clear that all applicants for membership will be judged on the basis of the copenhagen criteria and that all will be on an equal footing in this respect. turkey does not meet the political part of these criteria. there are still gaps in democracy, the rule of law, human rights and the protection of minorities. the question is how to ensure that the necessary reforms are implemented in turkey and that it is firmly and irreversibly committed to becoming a strong member of the family of european democracies. i am firmly convinced that this process will only begin in turkey and will only be successful if the signal to europe is green for turkey. turkey has made some progress in recent times - although it is by no means sufficient - in the field of democratisation and human rights and i would point out that this is clearly reflected in the next regular report on turkey. this regular report will be discussed in the commission next week, day by day, and a decision will be taken on it. he points out that the system of emergency courts was changed in june this year and that the military judge was removed from the so-called state security court. it notes that several important legislative and administrative measures have been taken to put an end to human rights violations by state officials. we expect turkey to take another important step towards abolishing the death penalty once and for all. i would also like to emphasize the rapprochement between greece and turkey, which took place shortly after the earthquake, on various issues of mutual interest and which is a promising sign for the future. i sincerely hope that the confidence created by the détente between the two countries will enable them to approach the delicate issues of regional security in the same spirit as has prevailed in the discussions so far. as you know, turkey has opted for europe and is ready to assume the obligations arising from the treaty of amsterdam. i therefore believe that the european council should make clear at its next meeting in helsinki what place turkey can occupy in the european structure. i would like to inform you today of the proposal i will make to the commission next week to recommend to the helsinki council that turkey be treated as a candidate for membership, on the same basis and in the same capacity as all other candidates. this means that turkey must comply with the obligations arising from the copenhagen and madrid criteria. turkey still has a lot of work to do and substantial progress is needed in the political and economic fields but in the long run, given turkey's enormous strategic importance for the future of europe, for security, stability and peace in europe, to refuse it admission to the enlargement process on an equal footing with the other candidates would be a grave mistake. we should, together with turkey, use the time that remains between now and the helsinki summit to agree on a timetable for turkey. the timetable had already been mentioned in the exchange of letters between chancellor schröder and prime minister ecevit prior to the cologne summit. specific measures in the areas covered by the copenhagen criteria which could help turkey to meet these criteria in the medium or long term would be envisaged. it is clear that any initiative in this direction by turkey in the run-up to the helsinki summit will contribute to the chances of success of this european council meeting. i am convinced that this parliament will play a vital role in the forthcoming debate, particularly when the overall process of legal alignment, of screening, is started, if it is decided in helsinki to grant turkey the status of a candidate for accession. to avoid any misunderstanding, i should like to make the following point clear: we are not talking about opening accession negotiations with turkey, but about taking the first step. this step consists in giving turkey the status of candidate country in order to start the process and to have the possibility, in the foreseeable future, to be able to discuss the subject of the opening of negotiations.
