counsel. - (fi) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, everyone knows that the multilateral trading system has guaranteed stable economic growth for 50 years. one of the european union's key priorities in its external relations is the strengthening and stabilisation of the multilateral trading system. the new round of trade liberalization is the necessary and natural follow-up to the results achieved previously. the european union has been advocating a round of enlarged trade negotiations since 1996. despite the fact that many countries had doubts about the benefits and benefits of a new round, all wto members are now in favour of a new round of negotiations. opinions differ, however, as to the extent of this trick. one of the major challenges facing the european union is to convince developing countries and civil society of the benefits of an extended cycle. finland, as the eu's president-in-office, will endeavour to ensure that a final decision on the date, form and agenda of the future round of trade negotiations is taken at the wto ministerial meeting in seattle in november and december. the most extensive possible cycle will ensure a balanced final result which takes account of the interests of all. as is well known, on the basis of the decisions of the uruguay round, negotiations will continue at least as regards agriculture and services. this is called the build-in-agenda. if we fail to convince the other wto members of the advantages and benefits of a wider cycle, the risk is that the negotiations will focus precisely on agriculture, where the european union has important interests to defend. the european union also agrees that the final outcome of the cycle must be adopted as a whole and by all wto members. in other words, nothing will be decided until everything is decided. this does not, of course, prevent some sectors from achieving results more rapidly than others. it will also be necessary to ensure that the results obtained reflect the views of all wto members in an equitable manner. there is also consensus within the european union on the duration of the tour, which should be around three years. it should be borne in mind that the european union's objective of an enlarged cycle must take into account both the sectoral and intrinsic agenda of the united states and its line towards lowering customs duties, and the more reserved view of developing countries. the developing countries have in particular called for a review of the uruguay round agreements and for them to be amended in a way that is more favourable to them. what is of particular importance for the success of the european union's objectives is that developing countries are convinced of the benefits of an enlarged round of negotiations and of the european union's good intentions underlying these objectives. this means first of all that the european union should be able to tackle issues that are difficult for it, such as dumping and the textile sector. in other words, the european union must be open to proposals from other wto members. instead of promises, the industrialized countries must be able to offer developing countries tangible benefits. the european union was among the first to advocate an exemption from customs duties for almost all products from the least developed countries, at the latest by the end of the new round. we hope that other industrialised countries besides the european union and more advanced developing countries will accept this objective. i will now briefly review the most important issues that the european union proposes to put on the agenda of the next round of negotiations. as far as agriculture is concerned, it must be possible to practice it throughout europe, including in regions where it faces particular problems. agriculture must ensure the survival of the countryside, the protection of nature and the dynamism of the rural world. these are all parts of a whole which we use the term 'multifunctional'. the european union, a major food exporter, also attaches importance to improving market access and removing trade barriers in the new cycle. we are also not prepared to negotiate a reduction in aid, provided that the so-called 'peace clause' and the so-called 'special safeguard clause' are maintained. in addition, it must be able to respond to consumer concerns about food quality and safety, environmental protection and ensuring animal welfare. the union also supports an extended wto cycle in the field of services. we believe that no sector should be excluded from the negotiations. the basic principles of the european union in the negotiations are the improvement of service commitments and the extension of existing commitments both by sector and by country. the european union considers it important that the participation of developing countries in the negotiations be supported by the possibilities provided by service contracts. the union considers that a rules-based system is in everyone's interest, as it avoids unilateral intervention in the course of events. we are in favour of the new round of negotiations being used to set up new rules and agree on principles also in areas which are closely related to international trade. these include environmental, investment and competition issues. our aim is to reform and adapt the rules of the game of trade so that they meet the requirements of a global economy on the path to globalisation and integration. in the future, the wto rules will have to be formulated in such a way that they provide the opportunity to ensure environmental protection and fair treatment of foreign investment. at the same time, it will be necessary to ensure that the special conditions of developing countries are taken into account and that they are allowed to move forward flexibly in the adoption of the new rules. sustainable development is a common objective of the member states, enshrined in the preamble to the wto treaty. trade policy and environmental policy must be more mutually supportive. the european union therefore considers it important that sustainable development is the basis of the negotiations and that the environment is taken into account in the different sectors of the negotiating round. foreign direct investment has grown faster than trade in goods during this decade. we want to create a framework that ensures that investments are treated without discrimination around the world. at the same time as the wto is beginning to work on an investment treaty that guarantees the rights of international investors, we believe that a mechanism should also be put in place to ensure responsible action by investors. the wto's monitoring work in the field of trade and competition is important for the european union. we consider that the definition of multilateral competition principles is an important element of the liberalisation of international trade, which in our view will remain deficient if it is not possible to intervene in the wto on the obstacles to competition put in place by a particular company and on the distortions of competition that these obstacles engender. in these areas too, the special conditions of developing countries will have to be taken into account and they will have to be allowed to make flexible progress. the european union is firmly committed to promoting democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights, including fundamental labour rights. the european union therefore considers it important that attention be paid to issues concerning the social dimension of trade in the next round of negotiations. it should be remembered, however, that developing countries are strongly opposed to the examination of so-called 'labour standards' within the wto. developing countries are concerned that these wto negotiations on fundamental labour rights are a way of tackling the relative advantage they have from low labour costs at home. it goes without saying that the wto negotiations must be based on a principle of openness. by being open on the inside, we will be strong and credible on the outside. we consider it of great importance that members of the european parliament should take part in the ministerial meeting in seattle. as the country holding the presidency, we will ensure that parliament is informed and we will take its views into account as much as possible. it should also be noted that contacts with non-governmental organisations have been strengthened both at community level and in the member states. we are living in a time of historical significance. a new millennium will begin with the start of the new round of negotiations. while this new millennium brings challenges for the wto, it will also reflect progress. the introduction of new themes in the wto is the answer to today's challenges. these new themes will help to move progress along the desired path. the presidency's objective is that the council's motion for a resolution will be adopted next monday at the general affairs council meeting. immediately after the meeting of the general affairs council, i shall be presenting a detailed commentary to the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy on 12 october on the council's common position in the light of the resolutions adopted. in conclusion, these resolutions are, by their very nature, the expression of the political will of the european union, which expresses a vision for the new millennium. the resolutions are addressed to the general public and at the same time confirm the general objectives of the european union for the start of the negotiating cycle on various substantive issues.
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, those of you who wanted today's debate on the seattle conference did not want, as i understand it, an exchange of technical words, but a political presentation. i think they're right. our public opinion is well aware that trade liberalization - which we want to take to the next level - is part of a wider movement which raises questions and questions and on which we must therefore take a stand. so let's really and truly ask the question: is globalization good or bad? the commission considers it to be a positive development for at least three reasons. first, the globalisation of markets makes possible the economies of scale which are essential to the industrial revolutions under way in information technology, biotechnology and transport. these advances are what must reconcile population growth and economic growth with a limited supply of natural resources, because it is technical progress that pushes back the frontier of the sustainable use of these resources. secondly, it is access to our markets and the liberalisation of direct investment that have supported the successful industrialisation of south east asia, opening up new and growing markets for our own exports and demonstrating that there are strategies to overcome underdevelopment. it is also the successes of the industrialized countries and the emerging economies in asia in liberalizing trade that have shaken the confidence of communist regimes and led to their radical transformation in europe and asia. finally, globalisation reflects the perceptions of the rising generations, those of the next century, who, through the media and their own travels, experience the world as a village where interdependence commands solidarity and where the taste for difference and encounter is expressed. of course, i do not intend to restrict myself to a lyrical or idyllic vision of globalisation. like many of you, i see the costs and risks of free trade without rules and without strong multilateral institutions to govern it. i see inequalities on the rise and even social exclusion in our countries. i see the growing gaps between continents. i see the instability of the financial markets. i see the threats to the local and global environment. but while our role here is to reflect the concerns, questions and expectations of our fellow europeans, let us keep in mind the global dimension of the challenges, those of the developing countries, which are today divided between the hope of integration into the world economy and the fear of marginalisation. it is also our responsibility to sort out the fears of millennialism, the resistance to change and the opportunities to seize in globalisation for growth, human development and environmental protection. through the negotiation of the new cycle, we are preparing the multilateral organisation of world markets for the 21st century, with the aim of achieving better balances. you know the reasons why the commission has proposed to the council and your assembly a long agenda and a short timetable for seattle. although i have taken this train of thought, i believe that liberalization through a round of negotiations rather than through the wto routine is desirable for three reasons. first, the liberalization of the card does not work. real progress requires big packages and one final commitment. this does not preclude the rapid acquisition of initial agreements when they are already mature. secondly, new subjects must be integrated into the wto's missions, subjects brought up by civil society: environment, culture, health, food, and also competition and investment, which are now inseparable from international trade. third, the global economy needs direction, after the financial crises that emerging and transition economies have experienced over the past two years. a round therefore appears to be the surest way of countering the temptation to protectionism. let us briefly examine these points. our position - and the presidency of the council has just rightly recalled this - is first and foremost concerned that the union should not be locked into a sectoral negotiation, which is included in the conclusions of the uruguay round, and which would only concern agriculture and services. our strategy is to balance the negotiation by opening it to all sectors, so as to cover our interests offensively and defensively and to encourage partners - and in particular developing countries - to do the same. on the agricultural front, the guidelines of the berlin european council on agenda 2000 provide a solid basis for achieving progress in liberalization compatible with the european agricultural model. the second is to define rules and strengthen the wto institution in order to strengthen its multilateral character, improve the impact of globalisation on sustainable development and prevent the environmental and health risks inherent in unregulated competition between different national standards and production levels. these rules concern first of all investment and competition, two subjects which some of our partners are hesitant about, for very different reasons, and which, because of the precedent of ami - whose initials i prefer to spell out - arouse reservations on the part of some developing countries and reluctance, or even radical hostility, in some of our non-governmental organizations. let me briefly explain both of these topics. on investment, let us be clear: we will not seek to impose on developing countries our investment codes, those which prevail in our country and which suit us. we want to convince them through negotiation that the most effective way to attract foreign direct investment, the preferred route to technology and international markets, is first of all to create a safe and predictable environment for foreign investors, whether they are from industrialised or other emerging countries. competition poses new challenges to all our economies with globalisation, the concentration of economic power and the extra-territorial impact of national competition policy decisions. but for developing countries it is an even more formidable challenge. these countries are faced with a double problem: their internal markets are too often dominated by monopolies or oligopolies, the first effect of which is to make local consumers, and especially the poorest masses, pay far too high prices, while the second effect is to block the arrival of newcomers and force them to remain confined to the informal economy. restrictive practices in access to markets, credit and energy are one of the main causes - generally not well known in our country - of underdevelopment, perpetuation of social inequalities and corruption in these countries. the inclusion of competition on the wto agenda is not intended to transform the wto into a global competition authority, but merely to establish a body of principles and procedures to promote the implementation of internal competition policies and to make them compatible with each other. let us now turn to three other themes: environmental protection, consumer health and the audiovisual sector, which, beyond the tensions between technical progress and cultural traditions, refer to features of civilization which distinguish europe: the requirement for quality, for example that of food, cultural identity in an open world, the preference for the non-market in a number of activities. it is clear that we suffer from a lack of rules and procedures in this respect, and i must say that this is the case here at home. the european union has set out to define policies to protect the environment, health and food safety. it is not enough to say that the commission is not prepared to take action in this area. everyone knows the complexity of these issues, which involve scientific knowledge with its share of uncertainties, national legislation and wto procedures. everyone is aware of the problem of the interface between national standards, wto rules and other multilateral agreements on the environment or health protection. with the new round, we must on the one hand prevent any abuse of these differences and divergences in a protectionist sense and on the other hand avoid leaving the markets to arbitrate between competing national standards. the precautionary principle must serve as a safety valve for us in regulating scientific uncertainties. furthermore, progress in labelling and product traceability, both of which are inseparable, would better inform consumer judgement. the european public also feels that it is necessary to strengthen the capacity for artistic creation in the audiovisual sector, a key sector of our culture, and the union must respond to this expectation. finally, i come to the issue that is most polarizing today between the opinions and governments of our member states, namely the link between trade liberalisation and progress in the fundamental rights of workers. for the european union, it goes without saying that these objectives are not only compatible but, in our experience, profoundly coherent. the return to free trade since the post-war period has been accompanied in europe by social progress, the two main vehicles of which have been the links of productivity and collective bargaining. in raising this question, we do not in any way mean to open up the possibility of setting wage standards or of weighing on the comparative advantages of developing countries, as mr sasi has very well said just now. we are also very aware of the risk of a protectionist drift which the unilateral imposition of social standards could potentially entail. nor do we want to make the wto the place for the development of these standards, the responsibility for which lies with the international labour organisation. our only concern is to advance in parallel the liberalization of trade and the respect, by our partners, of the fundamental social standards, as defined at the copenhagen social summit. in seattle, we must therefore try to convince the developing countries of the political legitimacy of this objective and of the interest of social progress in their own development. i have already referred to the developing countries on several occasions for two reasons. firstly, because the main target of this new round of negotiations is sustainable development and this concerns primarily the developing countries. secondly, because to achieve our objectives in this cycle, we need the consensus of all our partners and, of course, of the developing countries. but it is clear that this round should be seen in the wider context of global governance. a stronger and more rigorous link must therefore be ensured between the new pillar of the international system, the wto, and the pillar already constituted by the bretton woods institutions. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this debate on the new cycle you have called for raises an important question for me: does the union, through its own action, provide european governments and citizens with additional means to successfully adjust to and manage globalisation? are we willing, by exploiting our size, our weight in the world economy, the institutional advances we have made, to regain a sovereignty that the world markets sometimes contest and to contribute to effective global governance? if the council and parliament respond positively, our negotiating position will be stronger. this will mean that we are able to take the adherence to our opinions and to transform the fears we feel here and there into a project that makes sense. i hope that your parliament will one day be called upon to give its opinion on the results of the new round, which will require a lot of work and a lot of dialogue on our part. i am once again committed, on behalf of the commission, to continuing this dialogue with you on a permanent basis in the months and years to come.

president of the committee on budgetary control. - (de) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking mr napolitano for his good report and for his call for progress on this matter. anyway, i'm just stating the facts. more than a year ago, on 7 october 1998, an overwhelming majority, two thirds of the voters, voted here in strasbourg in favour of our colleague mr bösch's report on olaf and therefore in favour of the creation of an operationally independent anti-fraud office. in view of the criticisms already voiced at the time, we had demanded that olaf be an investigative body which deals objectively and without prejudice with cases of fraud or corruption. the first draft of the old commission was unusable. we demanded changes. then, in may of this year, we adopted the regulation governing olaf's activities with the council and concluded the interinstitutional agreement in question today between the three institutions - parliament, council and commission. for olaf, this agreement is, if you will, a "door opener". it lays down the rights and duties of persons concerned by investigations. in doing so, we are, among other things, giving a clear answer to the often debated question of insider information. in future, any official who has concrete evidence of fraud or corruption will not only have the duty to report it, but also the right to bypass the hierarchy and go directly to olaf if he deems it necessary, without any prejudice. another important point, which has been the subject of some controversy in the past, is the information of those involved in an inquiry. it'll have to be as fast as possible. in no case may any conclusions be drawn concerning the name of a member, official or employee without the person concerned having had the opportunity to express his views. the principle of contradictory examination is therefore perfectly clear. exceptions to this principle are possible only with the agreement of the president or the secretary-general, and again in very limited and exceptional cases involving particularly complex investigations in which too early information of the persons concerned could prejudice the work of the national judicial authorities. these are the two central elements of the interinstitutional agreement. they were approved in strasbourg on 6 may 1999 by a very large majority. the political decision taken at the time must now be enshrined in parliament's rules of procedure in order to allow it to have legal validity. i know from the conversations i have had that some members are afraid - as has also been expressed in this house - that olaf investigations could be abused in this way to put pressure on them, even though they are well aware that in the name of our credibility as members of parliament we cannot exclude ourselves from such investigations. two things about that. olaf does not annul the protocol on privileges and immunities which grants special protection to parliament and its work. the national judicial authorities will therefore still have to ask for the waiver of immunity, which will have to be decided by this house. secondly, we have taken all the necessary precautions to ensure the independence of the office in its investigative work, even though it remains a commission department formally and organisationally. as a political control body, we will intervene if this independence is threatened. that is why i take this opportunity to tell the commission that i find the recent appointment of a new head of division within olaf unacceptable. the criticism is not directed at the person named, whom i do not know, but at the fact that there has clearly been another attempt to put us in front of the fait accompli before the arrival of the new director. we have to reconsider that decision. - the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0034/1999) by mr lechner, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a european parliament and council directive on a community framework for electronic signatures (7634/1/1999 - c5-0026/1999 - 1998/0191 (cod)).
the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, if the internet used to be a means of information, its use has now been extended to buying and selling, not only for companies but also for mr. tout-le-monde. this rapidly growing market by its nature overlooks national frontiers and requires a community framework. the commission is aware of this and has put forward a proposal for a directive on a community framework for electronic signatures, i.e. signatures which are not in handwritten form but in electronic form. in january 1999, parliament approved 32 amendments at first reading. subsequently, on 28 june 1999, the council adopted its common position, taking into account to a large extent the amendments proposed by parliament. the committee on legal affairs and the internal market debated this common position and adopted it unanimously, with seven amendments. there is one, however, that we should not accept. i would like to address the following points: the directive is designed primarily for participants in open systems such as the internet and does not alter in any way the voluntary agreements concluded in the framework of so-called 'closed' systems. the internet does not stop at the borders of europe. the directive therefore aims at openness towards third countries and provides for cross-border agreements. secondly, the future of legal and commercial electronic transactions depends to a large extent on the confidence of consumers in improving security; the commission has also proposed that the court of justice should be consulted on the interpretation of the provisions of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. to this end, electronic signatures are a crucial prerequisite. this signature, issued in electronic form, can guarantee the identity of the author or signatory of a declaration. in addition, the integrity of the data transmitted can also be established. as regards the technical standards covered by the directive, the aim was to achieve technological openness. a higher standard of security should be achieved through advanced signatures and qualified certificates. the directive guarantees the community supply of the corresponding cryptographic products without allowing it to be subject to authorization. however, it does allow for voluntary accreditation schemes to improve the level of quality standards. the minimum liability of certification service providers is provided for in the chapter. the use of pseudonyms must be allowed and data protection must also be taken into account. as regards users' confidence in the reliability of legal electronic transactions carried out on the internet, a crucial issue is the legal effects of these procedures. in the future, advanced signatures will be legally equivalent to handwritten signatures because they are particularly secure. but in principle, the legal effects and the use of simple signatures as a means of proof cannot be disputed. with this directive, which is the first general regulation of its kind in the world, the european union is taking a decisive first step towards regulating and promoting electronic commerce within the community. it is likely to strengthen citizens' confidence in the reliability of open networks, in the services and products offered and in the legal value of transactions carried out on the internet. it also contributes greatly to the free movement of goods and services in the internal market, both for consumers - shopping on the internet; if i may mention a fact of interest to the general public - that for providers and producers of essential cryptographic services and products. i would like to thank the commission and the council in particular for their exemplary cooperation with parliament. i would also like to thank the members of all the groups in this parliament and those who were members of them in the previous parliament, which had carried out a lot of preparatory work. our task is essentially to dismantle, with courage, national regulations which are in disagreement and harmonize them. in this case, we are faced with a new technological and social reality in full development which we can inscribe from the outset in an autonomous european legal framework and which, in doing so, we can offer special protection as a european legal community. we must not allow the emergence or strengthening of national regulations which are not in line with the community's interests, beyond a certain margin of manoeuvre. for this reason too, i believe it is important that this directive should come into force as soon as possible and i ask you to approve it.
- (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, european regulations are often criticised for their lack of balance: they are too bureaucratic, or serve special interests, or are even ignorant of developments on a world scale. i think we can say that in this case we have a very good counterexample. legal harmonization always requires a difficult balance to be struck between the necessary harmonization on the one hand and the consideration of the legal traditions of the member states on the other. we have here a great example of balance. on the one hand, there are few but clearly defined rules on the requirements for electronic signatures; on the other hand, member states may decide in which cases they treat such signatures as traditional declarations of intent, whether in the form of a signature, a handwritten document or another official act. in this connection, i would like to stress in particular amendment no 2, which clarifies a somewhat confused wording in article 5 (1). i would like to emphasize once again that in the course of the discussions in committee we were all assured that there is no automatic link between an electronic signature and its transposition into formal requirements defined in the member states. the legislator is free to decide on the cases in which he equates an electronic signature with a handwritten signature. this directive is also a good example of balancing the interests of the economic sector on the one hand, and those of consumers on the other. first, we have a clear and simple rule that sets out only a few requirements. for example, consider the annexes. but on the other hand, we have the necessary protection in terms of the binding nature of these contracts and the liability of the service provider. finally, this directive is a good example, not only of the european union's consistent action at home, in the internal market, but also of its openness to international cooperation. we have a clear framework which is primarily of internal community value, but it should be noted that the text of the directive itself states that it is open to the establishment of international rules. in this particular area, it is very clear that community harmonization places us on an intermediate level in regulatory matters. we have the national level, we have the european level and for some time now, we have been adding the international level, more and more and in an increasing number of areas. in this respect, it is good that we make it clear that we are ready to address the issues of new technologies, of electronic commerce, on a global scale. it is clear that this will also have to play a role in the wto negotiations. as a new member of this house, i am pleased to have been able to make my first contribution to this excellent example of european regulation, which i hope will receive broad support in this house, and i also hope that the directive will be adopted without any problems in the council of ministers.

- (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too would like to begin by thanking mr lechner for his excellent report, which i can also support in full. with this directive on a community framework for electronic signatures, the european union is taking an important step towards eliminating obstacles to electronic commerce. until now, the legal consequences of electronic signatures have been unclear and the question of whether electronic declarations with a digital signature could be admitted as evidence in legal proceedings was particularly open. these problems will lose their importance at european level, since the directive will now also allow legally binding declarations to be made in electronic form and thus allow electronic commerce. the directive is the first step towards the creation of a comprehensive regulatory framework for electronic commerce. in doing so, it is, among other things, setting the course for the e-commerce directive, the distance selling directive and, to some extent, the copyright directives, both of which will soon be dealt with at second reading in the european parliament. my colleague mr wuermeling has already quite rightly explained that the directive leaves it to the member states to determine in what cases an electronic declaration with a digital signature is equivalent to a declaration with a handwritten signature or to a declaration for which the law requires, for example, the handwritten form. i particularly welcome the fact that the directive excludes national contract law from its scope - in particular, as regards the form and execution of contracts - and limits itself to the essentials. i would like to make two brief remarks on the directive. firstly, it is extremely important to create a european electronic signature system which is open to global developments and capable of integration. in this connection, the commission is particularly invited to contact third countries and international organizations to find appropriate solutions. in this context, particular attention will have to be paid to the proposals developed in this field by the un commission on international trade law (uncitral), the oecd and the wto. the objective must be the cross-border recognition of electronic signatures, which implies the creation of an international and compatible framework. secondly, i would like to stress - and i will end here - the importance and urgency of regulations on market access for certification service providers, the application of internal market principles and liability. it is high time that common provisions brought legal certainty to both certification service providers and consumers, who would then know precisely - as in the case of the use of credit cards - to what extent their liability may be incurred.
the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. i must say that this is the first time in this parliament that i agree with all the speakers. the debate was very constructive and different points of view were exchanged. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr lechner, in particular, on his constructive report. the progress made in parliament has also been of symbolic importance for future issues to be addressed in this area. the pace of technological change is such that we must strike a balance between rapid procedures and flexible legislation. if we fail, we will not be able to meet the demands arising from the upheavals we are witnessing every day in the various sectors of the information society in its various sectors. the directive on the agenda today deals with the use and legal recognition of electronic signatures. it is very important, and we have repeatedly stressed this today. the use of e-commerce by both businesses and consumers is increasing rapidly. the internet will be felt throughout europe in about five years. we can expect that by 2005 half of the european population will be connected to the internet, not only through personal computers but also, and increasingly, through mobile communication devices. that's the message that everybody got at the geneva telecom expo two weeks ago. the use of electronic signatures is an important means of ensuring authenticity in the future electronic world. without such signatures, european citizens will not be able to communicate securely by electronic means. in fact, internet use may even be curbed due to growing concerns about security and privacy. the fact is that without security and trust we will not see a significant shift towards commercial and financial transactions on the internet. this directive is not intended to regulate or replace the market in its entirety. it provides legal recognition for electronic signatures where currently only paper documents are recognised, thereby providing greater security in the market. it also ensures the security of the internal market for products and services related to electronic signatures. however, this initiative also has a considerable international dimension. the internet and electronic commerce are global in nature. this is why other international organisations such as the un and the oecd are becoming increasingly involved in the field of electronic signatures. almost all states in the united states have or are in the process of having legislation on electronic signatures. japan is also developing legislation in this area. a harmonised european legal framework would therefore strengthen europe's position at international level. this directive is also necessary to avoid divergent approaches in the laws of the member states, as has been mentioned. today, all member states agree on the importance of electronic signatures in ensuring security and trust in electronic communications. this is good news and we can reinforce it by avoiding obstacles to the free movement of electronic signatures in the internal market. as for the proposed amendments, the commission can accept all but one. amendment no 6 is a problem for us because, according to our interpretation, it is contrary to the treaty. it states that such a proposal must be submitted to the council. in this context, no mention is made of the european parliament. finally, i would like to reiterate that i am pleased with the high degree of consensus between the commission's and the european parliament's positions. it is in the interest of all of us to support rapid progress in this area. it is to this end that i would suggest to the european parliament that it reconsider amendment no 6 in order to avoid an unnecessary conciliation procedure. in this context, the treaty leaves no room for interpretation. thank you for your cooperation. i hope that this example of swift and consensual cooperation can be applied to many new initiatives in this area, already under discussion in parliament or to be discussed later this year or even next year.

year on the potential extension of the agency's activities to other balkan countries, under a new regulation. the second theme which has given rise to a number of amendments is the desire to place the agency under the sole and direct responsibility of the commission, which would appoint its director. in addition, independent experts appointed by the commission would replace the representatives of the member states on the management board. the management committee would be replaced by an advisory committee. this is what amendments nos 6, 12, 14, 16, 19 and 22 propose. the commission is of the opinion that the presence of the member states on the management board would be overall favourable to the agency and would facilitate the coordination of the reconstruction activities undertaken by the member states and the community. the commission would like to emphasize that this proposal is based on the standard model used for all european agencies, although the differences with the agency in question are notorious. this model shall include the representation of the member states on the management board and specific rules regarding the chain of responsibility. the management committee shall be constituted in accordance with the existing regulations. i do not want to conclude our plea in this way, however. the commission considers that a compromise which takes account of parliament's main concerns could be reached in the following way. first, the board of directors could be given an advisory role on certain issues, including project selection and implementation, instead of decision-making powers. secondly, in accordance with the parliament's proposal, the commission could be given the task of appointing the director of the agency. so what will be the next phase of events? i think that things are quite simple and i welcome what prime minister lipponen said earlier in reply to a question from a member. i shall pass these proposals on to the council and community action programme 'youth' for the period 2000-2004, which was forwarded to the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport. the commission proposal combined the existing youth programmes, 'youth for europe iii' and 'european voluntary service', and concentrated their objectives. our committee worked efficiently and quickly and unanimously adopted the coene report of 28 october 1998 with 61 amendments. on 5 november the plenary adopted the report at first reading. we wanted to strike a balance between the european voluntary service and youth for europe. the amendments proposed by parliament were intended to bring the programme closer to young people and thus to bring them closer to the european union. the emphasis we wanted to place was and is to increase the budgetary resources allocated to the programme - the commission had proposed 600 million, we 800 - in order to double the number of young people targeted. our amendments were intended to simplify the structures; improve communication with the target group; make the implementation procedures transparent; increase the participation of the least-favoured and the dissemination of information on the programme in order to improve access to it; the commission has also proposed that the age limit be relaxed and that a horizontal draft solution be found for comitology. the programme then remained stalled for seven months in the council before a result was reached under the german presidency by the publication of a common position based on a proposal for a programme of eur 350 million for a period of five years. this corresponds to an annual expenditure of less than 0.20 euro per capita on youth exchanges and is expressed as a percentage of the overall budget. i cannot imagine a european home without young people, nor can i imagine a programme which leaves most of them at the door. the european parliament therefore welcomes the fact that some of the amendments to the common position are in our direction. we have succeeded in imposing respect for human rights and the fight against racism and xenophobia in this programme. in cooperation with the commission, we have made it possible to take account of the elimination of discrimination in order to promote equal opportunities for men and women and there is also a user-friendly application adapted to young people. we have been assured that the european voluntary service is not a substitute for any potential or existing paid employment. i am now introducing 13 new amendments with the unanimous support of the committee, but these are again and again primarily about the allocation of staff, the duration and the call to the member states to remove the obstacles to access to the programme. first of all, the social protection and access to medical care of the young people concerned must be guaranteed, which could be arranged in the same way as in the context of student exchanges. in addition, there is talk of introducing a structure for collecting information on young people and creating a website 'youth in europe' and 'youth for europe' to reach new layers of young europeans through interactive means. all parties involved in the procedure should be clearly aware of the importance of this programme, which will take effect early next year, to reach our young citizens directly. the socrates and leonardo programmes have shown that a seven-year programme can be more effective than one spread over a shorter number of years. that is why i recommend that a seven-year programme be proposed and that the financial framework for this programme be set at eur 980 million. i propose a mid-term evaluation and an evaluation and re-evaluation of the youth programme. the success of this programme depends on an information practice that is not just for the insider. we must succeed in arousing the enthusiasm of young people for europe, in softening the peripheral situation of their countries, the social or financial problems they are experiencing and in awakening their appetite for europe. there will be no strict age limit in this regard. it is in diversity that europe's flavour and richness lie. i would like to call on the member states once again to commit themselves to social protection and health care. we respect the principle of subsidiarity, but the member states must also be responsible in this area. the time has now come to put the summit's fine speeches into action. in this area, informal contacts with the presidency and take our responsibilities. as rapporteur, i would do everything humanly possible to reach a workable compromise and i would invite the council to meet us, particularly on budgetary matters. the future 1999 to 2 may 2000. except for its extremely short validity - one year instead of three - and the increasing number of tuna vessels, this protocol is similar to the previous one. however, from a consider important.

union unless the community interest is put first. this is also why the macroeconomic dialogue is so important. this dialogue is not an end in itself, it serves to organise effective growth for employment within the european union and to help overcome mass unemployment. this is an element that is being incorporated into structural policies, into policies for the labour market. i wonder, however, whether we have understood the scope of this dialogue. in a society where work is highly shared, the activities of economic actors must be coordinated by the market or by political planning. promotion of cooperation with scientists from the new independent states of the former soviet union). a few years ago i was the rapporteur on this intas programme and i must say that it was a great example for me of how it was possible to create a cooperation network despite the adverse technical conditions, despite the inadequate infrastructure. it was also a very good example - i tell you, commissioner, in case you were not in office at the time - of the research policy being taken over by researchers, not always to the delight of the commission officials at the time! i think, however, that the experiment has borne fruit. we now have the eureka, cost, cist programmes based in moscow, and it is necessary that we develop a more formal framework for all this cooperation. that is also the meaning of this agreement. we will ensure that this agreement is really based on the principles set out in article 3. it must be mutually beneficial, since it is not a question of development the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, fortunately we are not faced with the same situation for argentina as for russia or china. argentina has definitely turned the military page of its history. it is a democracy today, cum grano salis, but it is a democracy. i would therefore like to recommend, as rapporteur, that this democratic aspect be taken into account in our scientific and technical cooperation. in other words, the argentine and european members, that is to say the european parliament, should discuss research and science issues and possibly put new emphases on these issues. argentina has made efforts in recent years to increase spending on research and technology, but it remains at a relatively low level. only 0.5% of the gross domestic product is spent on research. it is far too little, even though argentina is a leading country in latin america. but that is not the way to face the 21st century. in this context, cooperation between argentina and the european union is intended to encourage argentines and other south americans to increase their investment in the future. it is no secret that the share of latin america, and therefore of argentina, in world trade has declined substantially over the last twenty years. it is also because we are not investing in the future. the capital is fleeing, but the people who studied there, in europe or the united states, have also left the country and found work elsewhere. this cooperation with europe is therefore - i repeat - an invitation to look in the same direction as we do, that is to say, to invest in the future. however, the resources are limited. you will find in my report a list from the commission which shows that argentina has participated in the fourth rtd framework programme for an amount of eur 18 million. these are rather small projects, certainly very interesting, but small nonetheless, and 18 million euros is not much! when you have that kind of money, you have to try to attract other funds. i would urge the commission to use this limited amount to encourage investment in research by private companies in argentina and - i repeat - in other latin american countries. i have before me figures that give me hope. let us estimate them at the level of the european union. the german chemical industry spends 12.3 billion marks a year on research and development; another 5 billion are needed for research abroad, usually in the united states, but also in latin american countries and elsewhere in the world. in total, european industry spends perhaps 20 billion marks - 10 billion euros - on research efforts outside the union. if we could use the funds allocated here by the european union to mobilise private resources, countries like argentina would no longer just be europe's workshops, but would also participate in research and development. i would encourage the commission to take this approach. i therefore say on behalf of the committee for which i am the rapporteur that we will give our consent. furthermore, i would like to emphasize that, as with china, research is going in both directions with these countries, argentina and others. we also enjoy it. in this year of the 200th anniversary of alexander von humboldt's visit to venezuela, i would like to recall that he brought his curiosity, but also something of it back to europe, namely the knowledge of tropical plants and the geography of this interesting continent. in this sense, i also expect cooperation with argentina and other countries to be beneficial for europeans, for the european union.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, initially parliament gave me the task of writing a report on the guidelines for employment policies in the year 2000 alone. the overall discussion and the many suggestions made in the committee on employment and social affairs in a very general way concerning employment policy led to the decision to divide the draft report into two parts, namely a part devoted to the conclusions and a legislative part focusing on the proposals concerning the 2000 guidelines which will have to be adopted in december 1999 by the council of ministers. in doing so, we as parliament should try to focus on the essentials, so that the response from the council of ministers does not come back to saying that we would work more effectively by doing less. the council, following the vote in the committee on employment and social affairs, asked parliament for an opinion, which is now also official. the simple consultation procedure was therefore necessary. this means that legislative amendments can only be adopted without general conclusions. for procedural reasons, it was therefore necessary to submit two reports today: one on employment policy guidelines for the year 2000 and the creation of an employment committee, and a second on the joint employment report for 1999, which contains the conclusions adopted in committee. this second report opens with good news. the community's employment policy initiatives created 1.8 million additional jobs in 1998. however, youth unemployment and longterm unemployment are in most member states at unacceptable levels, since it is true that every unemployed person is one too many. i do not want to go into the conclusions in detail now, but in the light of yesterday's debate on the macroeconomic dialogue, i will mention one point: the european parliament must be more closely involved in the elaboration and implementation of the european employment pact. we regret that at the cologne summit the word 'parliament' was not mentioned in the employment document. this is unacceptable! we are the representatives of the people and therefore the most important body of the european union. the opinions of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities are attached to this second report. the two opinions have considerably enriched the work of the employment committee. i thank the rapporteurs for their opinions, mrs theorin and mr grosch, for their excellent work. many of their suggestions were incorporated in the two reports of the employment committee, but in the interests of concentration we had to make a choice. we are thus improving the chances of their being adopted by the council of ministers. the committee on women's rights has also dealt intensively with the employment guidelines, and this brings us to the legislative part, i.e. the first report on the agenda. again, it has two parts, firstly a proposal for a council decision establishing the employment committee and secondly a proposal concerning the employment guidelines for the year 2000. this employment committee should provide advisory support to member states in the coordination of employment and labour market policy. i have already referred to the request in my report on the employment guidelines to focus on the essentials. it is a mistake to increase the number of guidelines any further. instead, i call for practical implementation and verifiability of the guidelines and national action plans based on concrete criteria. a pure and simple increase in numbers does not create any additional jobs. quality rather than quantity must be the watchword of a modern employment policy. in the field of combating youth unemployment and longterm unemployment, the transition from passive to active measures can lead to effective and sustainable integration into the labour market. in concrete terms, the percentage of people receiving training, further training or retraining should be increased. we are aiming for a target of 25%, instead of the 20% proposed by the commission. we need vocational training in its most modern form. here, existing guidelines need to be adapted to the new requirements of the world of work, especially with regard to school equipment and internet access. special attention is paid to school-going and student women. a second approach is to provide access to the capital market, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises, which, thanks to their innovations, create the majority of new jobs. the encouragement of voluntary capital participation models for workers, coupled with a clear reduction in administrative expenditure and a determined fight against undeclared work, can be the source of job creation impulses. the additional costs must be reduced, since they have a direct impact on the competitiveness of small and medium-sized enterprises. existing or new concepts of energy taxation must, however, be tested to determine whether they are appropriate for maintaining the balance of the social security system in the long term as well. as a means of combating unemployment, the report also cites the enhanced adaptability of enterprises, which means that the cooperation of workers, their timely information and consultation and, therefore, their ability to adapt to change, must be ensured, for example by means of minimum standards. flexibility is also needed in working time. we want smart working models, like the breathing factory, where working time is determined by the degree of activity, reduced, most of the time, but not always, instead of unilateral reduction of working time with full wage compensation. it does not create new jobs but endangers existing ones. according to the commission's draft, the four pillars of the guideline continue to exist. the fourth pillar becomes the most important. this is the strengthening of measures to promote equal opportunities for women and men. the coordination of european employment policy, in particular through the employment guidelines, must initiate a long-term strategy to develop the social potential for creativity, innovation, creative minds, investment and performance. reforms to encourage dynamic competition and flexibility must be consistent with the need to maintain, but also to modernise, the social security system. this is how i see the european model. this is the model of the social market economy. it is in this context that i ask for the reports to be approved. the rapporteur. - (de) madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this directive closes a legislative procedure initiated under the auto-oil programme. ladies and gentlemen, together as the european parliament, i must say that we have made this legislative procedure a real success. we - the european parliament - have succeeded in making europe's air quality improve considerably in the future, since we have imposed a 60% improvement in europe and in particular in the cities. but it was not without its problems and we had to hang on to the conciliation committee. madam president, you were the head of the delegation that won this victory over the council. the council has clearly not dared to take the final step and has shown itself to be very reluctant on several points. the council has admittedly accepted some important points in its common position, such as the mandatory setting of limit values in two stages, the raising of the durability requirements for the pollution control systems of heavy goods vehicles and buses, the introduction of on-board diagnostic systems and a survey of vehicles in service. the council, on the other hand, expressed reservations on four points and i think that improvements can be made in this area. first, the council postponed the reduction of nitrogen oxide emissions from 2005 to 2008 and even added an intermediate stage before 2005. i think that this approach does not make economic sense, since everyone knows that nitrogen oxide emissions and particulate matter emissions necessarily follow the same evolutionary curve and that tackling one will automatically have an impact on the other. it is therefore not economically justified to set two different limit values in three years. on the contrary, a bulk reduction in nox emissions should be the aim. some claim that only technology can achieve this result. that's not true. several technologies exist to reduce both particulate matter and nox emissions to the level required by parliament at first reading, either by adding ammonia or by cooling the load in combination with a recovery filter. so it is not that solutions are lacking, and these solutions are not theoretical but prototypical. so we don't have to worry about the technical feasibility of these solutions. moreover, such a decision would be a waste of all the engineers' efforts and would make no economic sense. in addition, the reduction of nitrogen oxide emissions is of course also justified from an ecological point of view. why would you do that ? we are discussing, for example, a limit value for ozone concentrations, a value which we want to reach by 2010 and which would be 80% lower than the one currently recorded in the european union. if we really want to achieve this, we absolutely must also reduce nitrogen oxide emissions from trucks and buses. the european union currently has 168 million passenger cars and 23 million commercial vehicles and buses. these 23 million commercial vehicles emit the same amount of nitrogen oxide as 168 million cars, or 50% of total nitrogen oxide emissions. so we have to do something ! the second point on which the council was somewhat reticent concerns the issue of retrofitting old vehicles. we know that trucks and buses have a long life span and therefore travel long distances. it is therefore essential to provide incentives for retrofitting these vehicles so that older vehicles also become cleaner. the council also expressed reservations about the introduction of more environmentally friendly vehicles - we have proposed some additional provisions here - and about the introduction of strict controls to prevent the beating cycle that has been observed in the united states, i.e. that the manufacturer can easily circumvent the emission limit values requirements by electronic manipulation. we intend to return to the charge on this point. we have a chance to bring this legislative procedure on the reduction of exhaust gas emissions to a successful conclusion with a view to improving air quality. our proposals must of course be very ambitious to start a conciliation procedure. we want to come out of this procedure with a good compromise and it is therefore unthinkable to start with this compromise. let us therefore show courage here too, let us initiate a conciliation procedure as short as possible and let us ensure that our victory - the improvement of air quality in europe - remains a masterpiece to the end! the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal under consideration deals with the transmission of judicial and extrajudicial documents. at first glance, this might seem rather incidental, even uninteresting. most often, however, when a citizen wishes to assert his rights in the context of litigation, civil proceedings, he must first obtain from the partner, the contractor, the opposing party, documents such as the documents instituting the proceedings, replies, enforceable judgments or notarial acts, and this via a formal, legally demonstrable notification. however, attempts to assert rights are often thwarted at the first hurdle when they take place in a crossborder context, because notification procedures between countries are at best incomprehensible, complicated, slow, costly and subject to many errors. the international conventions on this subject - the main one being the 1965 hague convention - are full of numerous reservations by states, are very complicated and difficult to understand and apply. to improve this situation, the member states concluded a convention in 1997, on which parliament had delivered its opinion. however, this convention has not yet been ratified. the commission proposal is based on the convention. in doing so, the commission exercises its right of initiative in the community area of judicial cooperation in civil matters, pursuant to article 61c of the ec treaty and in accordance with the procedure laid down in article 67, namely a unanimous decision of the council of ministers after consulting the parliament. the united kingdom and ireland have expressed their willingness to be fully involved in the community's work on judicial cooperation in civil matters. denmark has so far not indicated that it too would like to participate in the procedure. as the title of the directive indicates, it concerns the transmission of documents in civil and commercial matters, thus excluding criminal matters. this is one of the many measures proposed in this area. as regards the substance, it must be said at the outset that the replacement of the hague convention and the successive conventions by a single, concise community legal act is already a major step forward. the legal situation is more accessible, uniform and transparent. the key points are that in future transmissions will have to be made in a decentralised and immediate way between the so-called originating entities and the required entities in order to avoid delays resulting from the involvement of several instances in each country. in addition, it is planned to set up central bodies to provide assistance in problematic cases. uniform forms will be drawn up at community level and common provisions will be made for the use of languages and translations, with binding deadlines. while the proposal represents a very remarkable improvement in the situation of crossborder judicial proceedings, it seems to me that it is still stuck in the middle. first of all, because a directive is being proposed. the appropriate instrument would be a regulation which would increase the binding nature of this legal act and avoid potential sources of error. the proposal also contains too many exemptions and special provisions which provide for derogations for states and which are a relic of the practices adopted in the framework of international conventions. it is difficult to see how such a large number of national derogations could be justified in the context of a procedure for the transmission of documents which should nevertheless be efficient and rapid. in sum, it is not a question of the integrity, which is absolutely worth protecting, of the substantive legal order of the states or of the equally justified protection which a state must offer its citizens in the event of a dispute, but of correcting and leveling the channels of civil judicial transmission between our countries, of making them shorter, better, but above all faster and, why not, cheaper. for these reasons, we propose a series of deletions and amendments aimed at abolishing such derogations or at least allowing them only in exceptional cases: for example, articles 2, 9, 12 and 15. some other improvements are also planned, for example in terms of translations, linguistic problems, costs and differences in interpretation between the competent authorities. i would like to thank the members of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market and the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs for their cooperation and for the amendments tabled. i also thank the commission for this relevant proposal which will make it possible to achieve a considerable improvement in the enforcement of the law at cross-border level. the proposal does not go far enough, however. you're taking three steps forward, so to speak, before taking a step and a half back. our amendments are designed to maintain the three steps forward and to abandon the three steps backwards - the exceptions and derogations. i would ask you to approve this and i would ask the commission and the council to take up our proposals in the interests of a better application of the law for the citizens of the union.
the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the creation of a uniform legal area is a basic duty of the european union. it shall provide citizens with adequate protection and security; i would even say serenity. otherwise, citizens will not feel at home in this growing europe and will reject it. the european legal area must therefore encompass more than judicial cooperation between member states on the basis of international conventions. it must be transparent, guarantee such a high level of legal protection everywhere and, above all, exclude any form of prejudice, even for procedural matters. the amsterdam treaty has made a great step forward. in principle, it has made civil judicial cooperation a community matter. the member states must now have recourse to european legal instruments in this field - that is to say, the regulation and the directive drawn up with the participation of the european parliament, the elected representative of the european peoples - rather than to international conventions. with this draft regulation in the field of family law, we now have an important component of the european legal area. we shall see when we have finished with this question because the commission has made a good proposal. i am not opposed to the need, as rapporteur, to have a number of amendments adopted unanimously by the committee on civil rights - please spare me the exact wording, which is unpronounceable. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me give you a little insight into the everyday life of our law. the abolition of frontiers between member states has not only created a european internal market that has brought economic prosperity. the abolition of borders also gave european citizens freedom of movement on a scale never before seen. more and more people are taking advantage of this new mobility. they get to know each other, discover each other, form partnerships, couples. love has its own rules and a rhythm that the law can hardly keep up with. this is shown at the latest in the case of separation of couples formed across national and legal borders. the former partners and the different legal systems are then quickly thrown into conflict, with all the unpleasant consequences of which the children are often the main victims. you all know the headlines that come out of the newspapers when such conflicts escalate to the abduction of one's own children. laws cannot prevent people from tearing each other apart and suffering the consequences. but laws can help to limit suffering and prevent further suffering from the application of divergent and inconsistent legal provisions. the subtleties of procedure may be enough to sow doubt in the minds of the parties, for example, as regards the jurisdiction of the court or the recognition of judgments. the regulation on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in matrimonial matters and matters of parental responsibility for joint children is an attempt to contribute, by legal means, to alleviating or avoiding the suffering resulting from the separation of couples. as rapporteur for the european parliament, i had to ensure that this necessary regulation achieved its objectives without, however, being as opaque to the citizens as its title. it is in this context that the amendments which, as i have already said, were adopted unanimously by the committee after intensive discussions, should be seen. at the end of the vote in committee, there was only one point of difference. this was the child's opportunity to be heard in the custody proceedings. i believe that it is absolutely essential that the child be heard if everything is to be done for his welfare. others believe that this objective can be achieved in different ways. since then, i have worked with mr watson to find a solution which takes account of both concepts. i am very grateful to mr watson for this, because he too has a particular concern for the welfare of children, who often suffer most from separation. i shall put the compromise reached in the form of an oral amendment to the vote and i hope that this house will also approve this procedure on this occasion. of course, this amendment will have to be adopted. there is another point which still needs to be worked on in the rules. however, parliament cannot take a decision on this matter and can only make a request. as you know, three member states do not participate in the legal acts under title iv, in accordance with the protocols of the treaty of amsterdam, and are therefore not bound by them. two of these states are nevertheless prepared to adopt the regulation under discussion. i therefore call on the third of these states to enforce this regulation as well. we would then have taken a significant step towards the unification of family law within the european union. in conclusion, let me emphasize three points on which it has seemed to me important, after many discussions with the parties and the judges concerned, to improve the commission's good proposal. first, in the event of a dispute, the welfare of the children must be given the highest priority and any other interest must be subordinated to it. secondly, litigation cannot lead to any form of discrimination. everywhere in the european union, the law must offer a high and comparable level of protection to every individual. thirdly, the jurisdiction of the courts must be clear and transparent. the recognition and enforcement of decisions may not be used for purposes of revenge. i think the commission agrees with me and i thank all those who, going beyond parliamentary routine, have helped me to draw up this report by means of constructive collaboration. i would also like to congratulate the council, which has also dealt with this matter and said that a good decision on this matter should be taken very quickly. security and justice.
