commission. - i am very pleased to be taking part for the first time in a debate in the european parliament with the high representative for the common foreign and security policy. we are all very fortunate that the main person responsible for developing a more effective and coherent european defence and security policy is mr solana. as you know, he enjoys a solid and well-deserved reputation on the international scene as a defender of the values which have been the source of the best in european history during this century, but whose absence has been the source of the worst in this same history. the high representative and i spent much of the first few weeks in our respective posts studying together the problems that were unfolding at the time on the ground, 30,000 feet below our airplane seats: we travel a lot. i am reminded that lord grey, who was british foreign secretary for ten years at the beginning of this century, has only been abroad once. if i remember correctly, this visit was followed shortly by the outbreak of world war i. i suppose lord grey was considered a great traveller. with all the travel we do today, we may be more informed than he is, but we may not be. i do not wish to go back on the various points which the high representative has so well developed, but since you have invited me to take part in this debate, which i sincerely welcome, i would like to say a few words about what the commission thinks of the construction of a european security and defence policy. security and defence, which are at the heart of the common foreign and security policy, are also, inevitably and rightly, dear to the hearts of the member states. as was clearly shown at the beginning of this week by the historic meeting - to use the adjective used by the high representative and the word is not too strong - of the general affairs council attended by the defence ministers, the member states are convinced that better cooperation within the european union in security and defence matters will have two major benefits. firstly, it will enable everyone to make better use of the resources available and, secondly, everyone will gain in power, precisely because the member states are working more closely together. these advantages are more necessary than ever in the field of security, because today we are making greater demands on europe. the rest of the world expects more from us, because we are doing well economically and we are doing well in the field of establishing peaceful and stable democracies. i think our own citizens expect more from us, who do not see europe in terms of balance sheets and gdp alone. how could they, given the frenzy of political events in recent years, a frenzy that began the day an american political pundit told us that history had ended? the european union must rise to the occasion. it's as simple and as complicated as that. the treaty of amsterdam and the cologne declaration present a formidable challenge. and we in the commission want to play our part in helping to achieve that. we have no military role. the gathering of so many uniformed men on the sidelines of the general affairs council on monday evening appeared to be an interesting cultural development. however, what the commission has is the means and experience to make a significant contribution to the non-military dimension of security. the petersberg initiatives pave the way for a comprehensive package of crisis management measures allowing for an interaction between community instruments, traditional diplomacy and, where appropriate, the use of military force. we are reaching a crucial point here. the military dimension is sometimes indispensable and decisive, but the non-military dimension can be just as essential. the nature of conflict has changed so much in this century of bloodshed. 85% of the casualties in world war i were soldiers and only 15% were civilians. in today's conflicts, the opposite is true. moreover, with the increasing sophistication and interdependence of our societies, aspects such as economic measures and the free flow of information have become increasingly important in conflict management and prevention. the european union must therefore consider its action by reviewing the whole range of instruments at its disposal, both military and non-military. if you want to measure our contribution as a community, look at the diversity of our operations in the balkans. we are obviously involved in areas such as humanitarian aid, rehabilitation and reconstruction. but there are many more areas in which we can intervene to prevent conflict and human suffering. i am thinking in particular of respect for the law, institutional development and trade policy. this is the kind of thing we are supporting, for example in kosovo, and for which we will be committing a further community contribution of eur 500 million at the donor conference in brussels today. what i am saying is that it is not necessary to make an extraordinary effort of imagination, or even to read between the lines of the treaties governing our activities, to understand very clearly the roles that the commission and parliament can play. the usefulness of a coordinated military and civilian management of the crisis, at the level of the union and between member states, has not only been felt in south-east europe. we also see this in the case of east timor. we must improve our capacity as the union and as member states to manage crises and to support the international organisations active in this area, which is so necessary, alas! the european council in helsinki is to consider an integrated approach to conflict management and the commission is fully contributing to this review. let me make a point that some may find a little too prosaic. in the context of conflict prevention and crisis management, time is a crucial factor. the new commission has started to try to improve the efficiency and speed of deployment of the instruments we have in case of a crisis. parliament has often asked us to do so, and rightly so. the task is considerable. in many ways, any progress on this would be by far the most important thing i could do for our far more heroic goals. i hope that we can continue to count on parliament's support to develop more flexible and faster procedures and i do not miss an opportunity to draw the attention of the council to this point, which i am sure the high representative will not object to. the commission's role in crisis management is clear, but it goes beyond this. it is not possible to develop a european security and defence policy without providing it with a competitive and open industrial and technological base, which is also in the interest of the european union's partners. we in the commission can help with a whole range of instruments in areas such as public procurement, the internal market, research and competition. i would like to make one final comment. we are sometimes talking about potential institutional conflicts in relation to the efforts we are about to make in the field of foreign and security policy. i hope i am not offending anyone, but i think the issues at stake are too important to be allowed to be emptied of substance by diplomatic jurists. it is clear that we must develop our foreign and security policy within the institutional framework of the union. it is clear that there is no clear division between military and non-military aspects. it is clear that the commission must play its full role in crisis management, even when there is a military dimension, because there will be a non-military dimension anyway. it is clear that the new structures must enable the commission to exercise its right of initiative fully. it is clear that the commission is not a body of amateurish officials and it is clear that we want to do a good job with the high representative, and with parliament, in providing europe with the security and defence policy that it needs and that the citizens are looking for. and if i have one more, i will say that it is clear that as long as i hold this office, i will not let high representative for the common foreign and security policy. - (es) mr president, in the few minutes we have left, i will try to make two or three general remarks on the questions which have been raised in this sitting. but first of all, let me thank all the members of the various parliamentary groups who have used their speaking time wisely and who have wished me or us good luck in this endeavour. i can tell them that i will use all my will, all my energy and all my political experience to try to carry out this task successfully, in collaboration with the other institutions. i think, as one of the speakers very rightly said, that the europe that is entering the 21st century is a better europe than the one that many of us dreamed of and that it still has a long way to go for the dreamers. it is undeniable that we have a single currency, that we have made progress in the economic sphere and that the time has come to make progress in the political sphere, and in particular in the sphere of foreign and security policy. and you will always find me working in that direction and in that light. i would like to make three points to sum up the many questions that have been raised. first, on foreign policy in the strict sense of the term. after the cologne summit, we have acquired new instruments - one of them concerns common strategies - which must undoubtedly lead to a profound change in the way we approach foreign policy. common strategies - some of which have already been defined - must involve pooling all the resources available to the union and the member states to carry out a policy. we have been lacking them until now. this is no longer the case thanks to the decisions taken in cologne and, very concretely, they are already part of a common strategy with russia. that must be our centre of gravity if we are to succeed. the second topic i wanted to address - as many of you have already mentioned - is concern about crisis management and prevention. i would like to say - and i will only refer to the lucid intervention of mr pierre schori - that i agree that it is not enough to get to the end and that we must try to prevent it from the beginning; that's what we're trying to do. the amsterdam treaty establishes an early warning unit whose purpose is to be alert to what can happen to try to prevent it from happening and not having to act militarily or collectively if we are able to do everything in our power through diplomacy, through prevention. let me share with you a personal experience that i have lived with great sadness. when we started to deal with the crisis in bosnia, there was a development in military planning, in the deployment of troops -- remember, 60,000 troops were deployed in bosnia -- that supplanted the civilian planning that should have been done. this difference in pace between the two has led to conclusions and consequences which we regret today and which i regret personally. in line with what has been said, i would like to see all the components - the civilian, police and military components - of any crisis management, peacekeeping operation planned with a global vision in mind. so the situation in kosovo would have been better today, and it would have been better in bosnia in the past. finally, i would like to make a brief comment on a current issue which - rule 97 (5) of the rules of procedure of the european parliament - give us the opportunity to follow and influence the work before the conclusion of the new agreement and to use our influence. a first expected results. our approach to negotiations must reflect our importance as the world's largest trading area and our responsibility for a global economic balance of interests, especially with developing countries. where should the emphasis be placed? what does it matter? the development of a global trade order? the opening of markets? the defence of our european economic and social model, the social and ecological market economy? community policies developed in the interests of citizens and consumers? in my opinion, everything, even if these elements have a tense relationship. all these objectives are equally important to the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, as the vote on monday evening shows. the european union must now achieve a greater opening up of world markets. customs duties must be reduced, technical barriers to trade must be removed. our markets should also be more open to developing countries, especially those with the greatest backlog, and to acp countries. citizens' understanding should be promoted and strengthened through greater transparency of the wto regulatory framework and dispute settlement procedures. on the other hand, the european union's obligations under other international agreements, such as those concluded with the world health organisation or the international labour organisation, must also be visible and respected. we are, however, opposed to unnecessary overburdening of the wto regulatory framework with other objectives than the main one of trade liberalisation and non-discrimination between the parties. for example, the core labour standards and social clauses adopted by the ilo in 1998 should be kept in a permanent forum between the ilo and the wto and included in the discussion, without changing the wto regulatory framework. if we start from the principle that fair and free world trade was the basis for the increase in prosperity of many states and their populations and in particular of the developing countries, we must also admit that the european union, as the world's largest economic power, has every interest in continuing this successful development and in involving more and more countries. to do that, we need allies. we must link our interests with those of the applicant countries and our neighbours in europe and with those of the developing countries, especially the acp countries. we also need a permanent dialogue with the american government, congress and people, a dialogue which shows the wisdom of our motives and which generates mutual understanding in order to strike a reasonable balance between our interests and those of our partner. through increased trade, we contribute to world peace, to well-being and, if we organise ourselves properly, to greater social justice. the extent of our responsibility determines our strategy. it must be global, promote a global balance of benefits and be convincing to our partners. the contracting parties must enjoy the freest possible access to all the world's markets. the rules in force in this field must be fair and based on mutual recognition of the advantages and observance of the obligations. the four fundamental freedoms of the internal market - free movement, free movement of goods, services and capital - must be globally valid objectives. we are in favour of the conclusion of multilateral environmental agreements which would then be taken into consideration in the wto. in the area of services, a growing market especially for european suppliers, market access and new sectors must be included. the european parliament should be consulted on this matter. we are in favour of sustainable integration and the promotion of electronic commerce within the gatt framework. the decisions of the uruguay round on public procurement must be applied. in the long term, many of the bilateral investment protection agreements will have to be replaced in the world trade organisation by a comprehensive multilateral regulation. competition in open markets must be more effective. the creation of competent authorities is necessary. the european model of sustainable agriculture, which is based not only on food production but also on the preservation of the countryside, the environment and our quality products, must be maintained. the attacks must be responded to in the light of the increasing aid policy of the us government. i would like to conclude with a comment on development cooperation. it must be updated and extended in the framework of the partnership with the acp countries. the world trade order is based essentially on the contribution of europeans and americans. in the 1960s, at the same time as the introduction of the common external tariff, we introduced a policy of reducing customs barriers and opening up the market during the kennedy and other cycles. the result was the conquest of new markets in third countries, but also the opening up of our markets to other industrialized countries. finally, i would like to thank the secretariat, our advisers and all those who have worked on this report in parliament. we didn't have much time. our technical services - like the others - have done an excellent job. - the next item is the report (a5-0058/1999) by mr dimitrakopoulos and mr leinen, on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on the preparation of the reform of the treaties and the next intergovernmental conference (c5-0143/1999 - 1999/2135 (cos)).
the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, the committee on constitutional affairs has discussed this report in detail at several sittings and i believe that we are presenting a substantial report to the house on the reform of the treaties. i must thank my colleague mr dimitrakopoulos for the excellent cooperation and also the division of labour which has enabled us to carry out this vast task. we agree that fundamental reform is needed before the union is enlarged to include new states, in order to preserve the effectiveness of the european union and, i would add, to improve the transparency and the ability to monitor decisions within european politics. we ask parliament to ensure that the reform we are about to see goes beyond the three amsterdam leftovers. these are important questions, but they are not enough. i would like to mention five points which i have made in my part of the report. firstly, we call for reform of all institutions and bodies, including the court of justice, the court of auditors, the economic and social committee and the committee of the regions. all these institutions must be put to the test. the reform of the council is the central point. in parallel with the intergovernmental conference, the council of ministers must carry out internal reform as called for in the trumpf-pires report, and the reform must be centred on the rule of majority voting in the council and, as a corollary, also on the co-decision of this parliament in all legislative acts. i think that parliament will also judge the intergovernmental conference on the basis of the success of this reform of the council. secondly, the intergovernmental conference must help to improve democratic control in european politics. parliament must be better able to control the commission and hold it to account. we are asking here that the president of the commission be given the opportunity to put the question of confidence to the european parliament and that the 'prodi procedure', whereby the president can dismiss a member of the commission, be inserted in the next treaty. thirdly, we believe that the reorganization of the treaties, which leads to a certain constitutionalization of the union, is now important. at present, no citizen or expert understands the treaties - they are not legible. if we want to be close to the citizens, we must unify the treaties into a single text and distinguish between two parts, a constitutional part and a second part, which must then also be partially subject to a simplified revision procedure. fourthly, the reform of the treaties requires not only an ambitious content but also a new method. a closed-door debate is no longer relevant and no longer acceptable. parliament must be involved in all phases of the preparation and conduct of the intergovernmental conference. in accordance with article 48, we call for the community method, we await a concrete proposal from the commission, which will serve as a basis for the negotiations, and an agreement with the council and the commission on the agenda and procedure for the next intergovernmental conference. article 48 is itself on the agenda of the intergovernmental conference. we believe that the union's dual legitimacy as a union of states on the one hand and as a union of peoples on the other must be taken into account by giving parliament a co-decision power in future revision negotiations when it comes to debating the content of future treaties. in this parliament we are ready to work together on a thorough reform of the treaties and to ensure that after enlargement the european union is still able to take the necessary decisions while remaining transparent so that citizens can understand and accept it. after the commission presented its proposals last week, parliament is doing so this week. many of my colleagues wanted to go much further, even calling for the drafting of a european constitution. we have exercised discipline and have been held within the broad framework of the institutional request. it is now up to the governments to show discernment and courage in helsinki to adopt an agenda which also aims at sound reform.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a regulation to the council. - (de) mr president, the report by our colleagues mr dimitrakopoulos and mr leinen is parliament's first statement of position on the tasks of the next intergovernmental conference. the framework is defined - without going into all the details - we know the challenge that the europe of tomorrow must face in order to be better understood and accepted by its citizens. the greatest challenge is undoubtedly the enlargement of the union, which we support and want. this enlargement to more than 20 member states - perhaps 30 in a few years' time - can be a strengthening of the union, but it can also be a weakening of it. it is a strengthening, because europe is consolidating its identity on the basis of its political and cultural history. but at the same time, such an increase in actors on the european stage would raise institutional problems and cause considerable operational weaknesses if we fail to implement adequate measures and radical reforms of the current system in time, before enlargement. the risk of paralysis of the decision-making capacity of the legislative power, council and parliament, and of the commission's inability to put laws into practice is a considerable problem, as is the difficulty of adapting the treaties to the ever more rapidly changing reality of the community. the two rapporteurs have rightly highlighted these problems and linked them to specific policy areas. the opinion of the committee on budgetary control seeks to answer the question whether the development of control and the effective protection of the community's financial interests must be tackled by the creation of a european public prosecutor's office in accordance with the corpus juris, while taking into account subsidiarity, as commissioner barnier explained to us last week during the brussels partsession. the report presented here is, on the whole, a step in the right direction, and i would like to express my gratitude to both rapporteurs.

are debating today contains parliament's proposals on the reform of the european union. this reform is necessary because of the forthcoming enlargement, but also because there is now a common monetary policy between, for the time being, eleven countries. this requires that the economic policies of the member states be conducted at least according to common principles. the economic system of the as proposed in the dehaene report - into an executive council of ministers which can deliberate behind closed doors and a legislative council of ministers which must meet in public. because in a democratic society, it is unacceptable that a legislative body is inaccessible to the public. this is unique in the world and cannot be tolerated any longer. that is why i think the proposal for the division of the treaties, as put forward by mr dehaene, is important. in the spirit of transparency and efficiency, we should group together the constitutional parts of the treaty, including the rules of jurisdiction, and put the rest together in another treaty of a lesser quality. this is also important, so that the citizen can understand how this europe is organized. this may lead to a starting point for the convention to draw up the charter of fundamental rights, and this convention may develop into a constituent assembly, because a constitutional contract is the long-term goal we must strive for.
- (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, believe it or not, but exactly 200 years ago, in 1799, the first discussion took place on a constitution, not for europe, but for bavaria. the reasons for this were, among other things, the establishment of competences, but also the profound territorial reorganization of an increase of almost 83 subdivisions of the territory. the main author of this idea was the minister of state of the time, count montgelas, to whom the merit of the establishment of a french administration in bavaria was attributed. however, he was also the strongest opponent of popular representation, as it could introduce into politics elements that were supposedly unpredictable. the supporters and opponents of this idea fought for another 18 years until the constitution was finally created and the opponents were finally eliminated, and this constitution already contained democratic elements. amazingly, the basis for the constitution of that time was a preamble drawn up in 1799 that set out basic rights - 200 years ago! the parallel with the subject of our concern today is astonishing. history shows that the arguments of skeptics then and now are almost identical. let us learn from history so that we do not let another decade pass before europe has a constitution. we must prepare europe for the future. i would therefore encourage the council not only to respect parliament's proposals but also to embrace them. we need a europe that is able to act, but also to take the necessary decisions. because we must also take democracy seriously, and the powers which have been entrusted to us by the national parliaments must be handed over to parliament, that is to say, entrusted to codecision. we need the co-decision of the european parliament, because the european parliament is the greatest factor in the integration of europe.

commission. - i shall reply quickly to the three points that have been raised: the death penalty, minorities in kosovo and the nikitin case. first of all, as regards the question of the death penalty, i should like to say a few words about the substance of the matter, which you address in your draft resolution and which, of course, is agreed by the commission as regards the position on the death penalty. i think that this does not deserve a long commentary, and we agree on that. i would like to address a specific point that was raised during the discussion, namely the draft resolution on the death penalty which the union had tabled before the third committee of the united nations general assembly. this is indeed a matter of foreign policy. in this resolution, the european union proposed that the international community commit itself to a moratorium on capital punishment. for us, the abolition of the death penalty is an intrinsic part of our human rights policy, whereas for many countries this issue - or at least this is their thesis - is exclusively a matter for criminal cases. we have indeed withdrawn this draft resolution after careful consideration, and this decision is subject to your assessment. we withdrew this draft because we felt that the discussions in this third committee of the un general assembly were taking a wrong turn. we have considered that some of the many amendments tabled by countries which have a problem with our position are unacceptable to us, in particular the amendment to insert in this resolution a reference to article 2 (7) of the charter of the united nations, which states that 'no provision of this charter shall authorize the united nations to intervene in matters which fall essentially within the national competence of a state'. this amendment was indeed inconvenient in that it moved the debate to another area, that of the national jurisdiction of a state. in our view, the introduction in the resolution of a specific reference to the principle of the sovereignty of states would have entailed a risk of calling into question the acquis within the united nations system, and in particular the 1993 world conference, which provided that 'the promotion and protection of all human rights is a legitimate concern of the international community'. furthermore, accepting such an amendment could have had a very negative impact on the work of the united nations in the field of human rights. so it is not, as i have heard, to give in to i don't know what pressures that we have preferred to close the debate in this way, at least for the time being, but to preserve a position of principle. this decision should therefore not be seen as the absence of a foreign policy, nor as a sign that we have succumbed to this or that pressure, but as an assessment by the union of the risk that, in the light of the proposed amendments, we would find ourselves, in the name of this legitimate fight that we share, somewhere below the level of those we had previously won. so that's the explanation i wanted to give. i now come to the second point, mr president, which concerns the rights of serbs and other minorities in kosovo. i believe that the commission and, with it, the whole of the european union have made it clear from the outset that we condemn all ethnic violence, whoever is the perpetrator and whoever is the victim. this violence is as unacceptable today against the serb and gypsy minorities as it was when it was perpetrated against the kosovars a few months earlier. through its assistance programmes for democratisation and human rights, the commission continues to support measures to restore trust and foster dialogue between different communities. we have already been doing this, unfortunately without much success, since before the conflict - and i agree with the indications given by many of you that we must all make a fairly serious examination of conscience in this matter. now, in new circumstances, we are trying to continue to act in a pragmatic way in accordance with these objectives, especially when selecting aid and assistance projects. we fully support the efforts of kfor to maintain law and order in kosovo and to protect all citizens. we also fully support the efforts of unmik to establish an operational civilian administration capable of carrying out the police functions currently carried out by kfor and to create a peaceful multi-ethnic society capable of taking on the reconstruction of kosovo and the re-establishment of its society. unmik has approached the commission for funding for the kosovo protection corps and the member states will take a decision in the coming weeks on the programme we have suggested in response to this request. we also support, in the form of partnerships, the efforts of unmik at the level of local administrations. in this context, we call on all people of goodwill in kosovo and beyond to also contribute to these objectives and help us ensure that minuk and kfor achieve them themselves. i would remind you that we are opposed to the partitioning of kosovo. it must become a multiethnic society, without distinctions or discrimination on ethnic or other grounds.

commission. - mr president, i shall take the remarks on which i owe you an answer, first on rwanda and then on burundi. as regards rwanda, the commission shares the concerns that have been expressed about the effectiveness of the judiciary, and i use this diplomatic word to judge the perpetrators of the genocide. no national reconciliation is possible without a real judicial process, and this concerns both the rwandan national judiciary and the international criminal tribunal for rwanda. in reply to mrs ries, as regards the rwandan national judiciary, the commission has focused its interventions on institutional support to ministries in strengthening the right of defence and civil parties, in improving living conditions in prisons and in supporting genocide survivors, as well as in respecting human rights. however, 130,000 detainees are still in prison, accused of genocide-related crimes, awaiting trial. the rwandan government is looking for alternative solutions, which leave no room for impunity and which are in line with our wishes. he is working on the definition of a system of arbitration courts in line with traditional practice, where the courts are made up of citizens elected at different levels of local administration, and they would be to judge three categories of accused: ordinary murderers, on the one hand, beatings and injuries without causing death, on the other, and looters, finally, so that the instigators and ideologues of genocide and massacres are actually tried by ordinary courts, which is somehow to organize in order to face this task. the commission is currently assessing with the other donors whether and how to contribute to the establishment of this system in the context of our cooperation. the commission has provided funding for the international tribunal for rwanda since its inception, to date amounting to eur 1.5 million. the commission will launch an evaluation of human rights programmes in developing countries. particular - the next item is the report (a5-0051/99) by mrs rühle, on behalf of the committee on budgets, on the proposal for a council decision granting a community guarantee to the european investment bank against losses under loans for projects outside the community (central and eastern european countries and the western part of the balkans, mediterranean countries, latin american and asian countries, republic of south africa) (com (99) 142 - c5-0039/1999 - 1999/0080 (cns)).
the rapporteur. - (de) i thank all those who have waited so long because today's sitting was relatively busy and for a long time we did not know when the report would be submitted to the plenary. i would like to see us reaching a decision today and tomorrow on the terms of the community guarantee to the european investment bank, the eib, because we would like, if possible, to take a decision before the council and also to proceed with certain amendments which i will come back to in detail. these guarantees concern the countries of central and eastern europe, the mediterranean countries, the countries of latin america and asia and the republic of south africa. my proposal is for a period up to 2003 - to be precise, 31 january 2003 - followed by a mid-term review and further discussion and possibly an extension until 31 january 2007. the proposal concerns an amount of eur 9 745 million and a guarantee of up to 60%. these points are not controversial; the controversy is about other things. the main problem with my report was that in the course of the work it became increasingly clear that the european investment bank was somewhat behind in terms of modern management, transparency and public relations work. some people have told me that the european investment bank is 20 points behind the world bank in terms of business management. i therefore think it is important that we look at this issue more closely. the european investment bank is the largest public bank in europe. its main owners are the member states and it primarily deals with soft loans. the bank enjoys high confidence on the capital markets due to the low interest rate expectations of the capital holders, which allows for a reduced gearing rate. the gearing rate, the ratio of borrowed capital to equity, is 2.5, whereas it is usually 10 on the market. this high level of confidence enables the eib to obtain loans on the most favourable terms on the capital markets and to subsequently grant loans at equally favourable rates. in addition, the bank enjoys tax exemption and, as a significant advantage, cash from the eu budget to cover political risks. despite this direct and indirect support from the european union to the bank, the bank likes to present itself as a completely normal bank to public opinion and has thus previously justified to public opinion its relative inaccessibility to collaboration and control in relation to other public institutions such as the world bank. we believe that this must change very quickly. that is why my report also deals with, and above all, the issues of accountability and transparency and, as i have already said, a modern business culture. in recent years, criticism has mounted against the eib's internal administration and business management. however, the bank has long refused to allow the court of auditors or olaf to examine its books on the basis of the bank's specific character. the eib's particular intransigence on public oversight and transparency issues even led the ecofin council to conclude on 8 october 1998 that, in view of the important financial role assigned to the eib by the treaty and a number of community regulations, the eib should take an exemplary stance in the fight against fraud and allow olaf to carry out investigations within it, where appropriate. the council is confident that the bank's governing bodies will shortly submit to their board of governors a draft decision in accordance with the interinstitutional agreement. the first signs that the bank is ready to open its books are now being noted. in my view, however, they are still insufficient and mistrust persists. this is further reinforced by the way in which mr blak, the rapporteur for the committee on budgetary control, has been treated so far, and whose questions have long been awaiting an answer. in this connection, i would like to thank the committee on budgetary control once again, and in particular mr blak and mrs theato, for the preparatory work which enabled me to complete this report in a short time. in future too, we will have to keep a critical eye on the eib's progress towards greater transparency, and i would point out to all those who are sceptical that profitability is also at stake. a closed, compartmentalized company makes its decisions on the basis of only a limited amount of information. the dialogue with civil society, as now practised by the world bank, among others, also provides insights into investment decisions. the bank has also been criticised on this point in the past, whether for its investments in the health sector in my country, which have mainly helped to anchor obsolete structures, or in the transport and environment sector in eastern europe. in future, it cannot and must not be enough for the bank to limit itself to the isolated examination of specific projects - for example, a section of a motorway - but it must also examine projects in a context - for example, within a national transport development plan - in order to identify possible duplication and develop an acceptable and more financially sustainable alternative. to this end, the bank must conduct aggressive public relations work in the regions receiving its assistance. the european parliament should therefore be attentive to the development of the eib in the coming years. the basis is laid in my report and i hope that it will be adopted tomorrow. thank you. i have a little bit overrun my speaking time, but i wanted to make clear the purpose of this report because for most people it is just specialist jargon.

by anti-competitive practices. if it is established that industry is suffering from any form of anti-competitive practice, the commission shall, where appropriate, propose to the council measures to remedy the problem. the first report shall be submitted to the council by 31 september 1999 at the latest.' in accordance with this obligation, the commission has drawn up its first report which concludes that the shipbuilding sector in the world market is facing serious overcapacity problems. the situation continues to deteriorate with the incessant increase in capacity, the increase in competition and the fall in prices. the report examined in detail nine contracts awarded to korean shipyards and concluded that none of them were awarded at full cost prices, which is causing a detriment to eu shipyards. the report suggests that action be taken by the member states and the imf-world bank to see whether the conditions of the (imf-led) rescue package for korea are fully met in the case of the yards. industry, member states and the commission should gather all necessary information that can serve as a basis for the preparation and filing of a complaint for an obstacle to concerned should strive to create a level playing field for the whole sector. the industry council considered the commission's report at its meeting on 9 november 1999 and published its own systems and, above all, in air transport capabilities. in this respect, europe is far from being self-sufficient. the helsinki european council is also to decide on the new bodies needed in connection with crisis management: political committee, security committee, military committee, civilian crisis management coordination body and military staff responsible for analytical work. the cologne the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam commissioner, the directive under consideration is the second daughter directive drawn up within the framework of the directive on the assessment and management of ambient air quality and the proposal is part of a package of integrated measures to combat air pollution. i think we can all agree that the citizens of europe should breathe cleaner air. in its most recent publication, the european environment agency notes that most cities suffer from air pollution harmful to health and that nearly 40 million people living in europe's 115 largest cities are exposed to at least one harmful substance above the who air quality guidelines. despite policy initiatives to reduce pollution and improve air quality, over the next ten years, the need for transport for people is expected to increase enormously and the number of vehicles to increase by 25%, further worsening our air quality. in a report published this year, who concludes that air pollution from transport causes more deaths than road accidents. the costs to the economy are also high. it is therefore important to reduce the level of air pollution in order to reduce its impact on the most vulnerable groups of the population and to relieve the burden on health systems. the essential element of this second daughter directive is that for the first time limit values for benzene and carbon monoxide are laid down in the eu. this is a very important step, i would even say a step in the legislation on air quality: for the first one, a limit value is defined for a carcinogenic substance, namely benzene, which can cause leukemia. we know that the sources of benzene are petrol and oil and in the european union 80 to 85% of benzene is produced by the combustion of petrol in road traffic. at present, there is no threshold value for the health risks of this substance and therefore no harmless benzene pollution. the principle of prevention enshrined in the ec treaty requires, however, that the threshold value be set at the level of an extremely low risk of disease. the commission has proposed an annual average limit value for benzene of 5 μg/m3, to be reached by 2010. this proposal has the full support of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy. the commission's proposal provides that in the event of so-called socioeconomic problems, countries could request a transitional period of five years, which could then be extended for a further five years. the committee on the environment expects the directive to be implemented correctly and proposes to limit the derogation to a single five-year period, with the 10 μg value to be respected during this period. other amendments tabled in the plenary make this derogation subject to additional conditions in order to avoid - and this must be very clear - that these regulations become an open door for not implementing this directive. the committee on the environment therefore wants to make it absolutely clear that this cannot be interpreted as a double-edged environmental policy. in the context of enlargement, i think it is essential that we set a good example in this area and do not send a bad signal to the applicant countries. the commission's proposal for a more precise and stricter derogation regulation would make it clear that it is not a question of pursuing an ambiguous environmental policy but rather of achieving a high level of protection for all eu citizens. the commission also proposes that in future public opinion be better informed and that the proposed measures be supplemented by other measures. i think that if we succeed in this, if - let us hope - the commission can agree with our proposals, we will have really taken a step forward in improving air quality and helped to make people understand that carcinogens cannot be dispersed in the environment. we want to improve the quality of europe's air and thus make a major contribution to health protection.

commission - madam president, the seattle conference ended in failure. why would you do that ? i see two reasons for this, one circumstantial and the other substantial. you know the circumstances. first, the conference failed because of lack of time. there was only friday afternoon left, which was too short a time to reach a conclusion in a reasonable time. this is due to the way the conference itself has been conducted, which has only allowed for genuine negotiations during the last two days. there was also, as another circumstantial reason, a clear inability on the part of some delegations to engage in a genuine process of negotiating the agenda and, in this respect, one has to ask whether the coincidence of the opening of the conference with that of the election campaign in the united states was a happy one. it has become clear that the country is not prepared to make any moves on any subject, which by definition makes it difficult for negotiations to succeed. as far as substance is concerned, i believe that the failure of the conference is due to the gap between the ambitions of the world trade organization and its means. the wto procedures have proved ill-suited to the need to integrate at the same time new actors, that is to say a growing number of developing countries, who are demanding their place at the table, and new issues, which are beyond our traditional agendas. you know these new topics: environment, social norms, for example. given the number of actors and subjects and the substantive differences between a number of participants, the chances of reaching an agreement were very slim. if we stop for a moment to consider this fundamental reason, i think we must recognize that the wto no longer has to monitor a negotiation of liberalization between industrialized countries and that this situation has been changed in two ways: firstly, it is no longer possible to limit ourselves to lowering tariff and non-tariff barriers to trade. we must be concerned about the impact of this liberalization on the main parameters of our development models, the fundamental rights of workers, environmental and health protection, cultural diversity, multifunctional agriculture, environmental quality. and then it is no longer possible to confine the negotiations to a few actors, the union and its friends, the united states and the cairns group. in seattle, more than in the past, we had to count on the major partners in the third world, india, brazil, south africa, egypt, the emerging economies, especially in south-east asia, and also our acp partners. tomorrow we will probably have to reckon with china as well. the combination of new subjects and new actors opens up very rich prospects for progress towards a controlled globalisation, but the difficulty of this undertaking is obvious. the union had prepared well for seattle, in terms of the subjects to be discussed, by advocating a broad agenda that met the expectations of civil society, which your parliament, the elected body and legitimate representative of that society, had advocated. as well as extending the negotiations to all partners, including developing countries, the european union also took the initiative of opening the conference with an offer to ensure that the least developed countries have broad access to the markets of the industrialized countries at zero duty. it has managed to rally japan first, and perhaps the united states and canada later, to this initiative. but let us not be deceived and keep our eyes wide open. what middle-income developing countries and emerging economies will demand in return for joining our social, environmental, health, workers' rights agenda is substantial improvements in access to our markets. and seattle has shown that we still have to convince these countries that our concerns, your concerns, are something other than the defense reflexes of a comfort that often appears to them as a privilege. a word about the strategy of the european union in seattle. the community is well placed to build bridges between the positions of the industrialized countries and the developing countries. we have shown this in seattle, where we were well prepared, both in substance and politically, and where we enjoyed what i believe was valuable support from both the council and parliament. we stayed together and at the same time open. from time to time we have moved, if deemed necessary, to move the negotiations forward. this was the case, for example, with the biotechnology group, which i thought it would be useful to accept at a certain point. this has been strongly criticised by some member states and by some members of parliament. i take responsibility for the risk

commission. - mr president, i should first like to thank all of you who have supported me, both during the conference and today. i am particularly sensitive to this because i think it is a method and a style of work rather than a personality, and that it is this method of work that will be useful to us in the future. in any case, i conclude that this is the direction we must continue in. i shall now make a few observations on the substance. first, as many of you have said, it is probably among the developing countries that the failure of seattle has caused the most disappointment. if we accept this fact - which i believe is now proved with a week's delay - it is when trade liberalization is decided, steered, controlled that the developing countries perceive its interest for them, and doubtless consider it better for them than a status quo in which the development of bilateral relations does not play in their favour. i think that's worth thinking about for the future, and at least between us. my second comment concerns the institutional affairs of the wto. i am not one of those who think that this is the main problem. i think that is part of the problem. we're not reinventing the wheel, but what good is the wheel when it stops turning? at least let's get this wheel to turn, or the load it carries to be reworked. i think that is what is at stake, while recognising - and i believe the commission does - the extreme difficulties that will arise in getting 135 contracting parties to agree on an institutional system other than the one that currently exists. a third observation concerns the environment. i listened and heard what you said. let us simply be aware that our ambitions in this area are considerable compared with those of the other partners around the wto table. the fact that developing countries have a less ambitious environmental agenda than ours will make it clear why. the fact that the united states - and it does - has a less ambitious environmental agenda than ours certainly poses a more difficult problem for us, because if we have neither the developing countries nor the americans on our agenda, then we will have a very difficult time getting it forward. i think that's worth thinking about. i stand by our creed and the council's conclusions, as well as the mandate i have received. however, we must be aware that this will not be easy and that at some point we will need to be more convincing or more active. this brings me to my fourth and penultimate observation. i think, as many of you do, that it is now up to the developing countries to direct our efforts to persuade them and to build alliances. this requires persuasion, political work, argumentation and perhaps some additional efforts which will have to be considered. i am not able to give a good picture of the situation at the moment, but it is certain that these additional efforts will have to be directed towards opening up our markets to these developing countries. i think it is useless to talk about it for long if we are not a little more specific, but i also know that if we are a little more specific we are faced with enormous difficulties. we must think about this and, in due course, put forward some proposals to the council and parliament on this point. finally, i would like to raise the issue of transparency. yes, seattle was a transparency event. we can think long and hard about whether there is always a coincidence between extreme media concentration - as in seattle - and an exercise in transparency. i must say that, on a personal level, i sometimes have some doubts and a little concern about this coincidence, which we too often try to recognize, between a massive media presence and an exercise in transparency. let's put that aside. nevertheless, the wto was subjected to a test of transparency in seattle, for which it was clearly not prepared. from this point of view, it's all the better. what we have to say about liberalisation, about globalisation, about how we see it, and whether or not it is good for the citizens you represent and to whom we are accountable, well, that's all the better. i am glad that this debate can take place in the open. i think, as some of you have said, that europe has an interest in this debate because, as far as it is concerned and in this area, it is used to it: it is as much a matter of taking advantage of others. court of auditors - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am very pleased to present to you today the annual report of the court of auditors for the financial year 1998, one of the fundamental elements of the discharge procedure. the discharge for 1998 is being given in a very different context to that of last year. our institutions have been both actors and witnesses to the major events that have taken place on the european stage. for the first time in history, the commission resigned during its term of office and, for the first time, political attention was focused on the management and control of european funds. the european union is suffering from a fundamental problem linked to a period of growth. the structure of the commission has not kept pace with the ever-growing number of community policies and funds which need to be implemented. the reports of the committee of independent experts make it clear that the commission's organisation, staff policy and procedures have become obsolete and do not allow for the production of policies characterised by a high degree of efficiency and accountability. this gap leads to weaknesses in financial management and control, weaknesses which the court of auditors has repeatedly pointed out. i think there is general agreement on these observations. the crucial corollary, in my view, is that all the european institutions and the member states must share responsibility for this situation and we must therefore work hand in hand to improve it. to this end - and this is part of its contribution - the court of auditors sent a letter to president prodi on 15 july this year, when he was still president-designate. it drew his attention to these basic improvements which were considered by the members of the court of auditors to be the most essential. this includes developing methods for assessing the effectiveness of policies, strengthening control structures, establishing simple and more coherent financial and accounting regulations and, finally, managing staff more effectively. the reports and special opinions adopted by the court of auditors during the year in the 1998 annual report submitted to parliament provide further evidence to support this analysis. as you have seen, the report now before us contains the insurance declaration for 1998. in response to parliament's requests, the court of auditors has extended its work to the declaration of assurance. it now provides additional information by revenue and expenditure sectors in each chapter, which will enhance the usefulness of the report in assessing the situation in each area. the general conclusions of the 1998 insurance statement are not fundamentally different from those of the previous year. firstly, the court of auditors considers that, overall, the reliability of the accounts reflects the community's position at the end of the year as regards its revenue, expenditure and financial position, with some reservations, however, relating to the omission of claims and potential debts, the overestimation of commitments still to be settled and the presentation of advances as final payments. secondly, the court of auditors is giving an increasingly unfavourable opinion on the legality and regularity of the transactions underlying the commission's payments. the audit revealed a significant level of error affecting the amount of payments made or the eligibility of the operations financed. the audit also revealed other breaches of the regulations. although these have no direct influence on the amount of transactions, they often highlight a problem with the correct implementation of control procedures. the court of auditors audited the final recipients of the grants and thus discovered a significant number of errors. this shows that not only the commission but also the member states still have difficulties in administering and managing community programmes. the commission and the member states have now started to reform the major spending areas, including agriculture, the structural funds and the phare programme. the achievement of real progress will depend on the extent of fundamental changes to member states' systems and also, in many cases, to certain council regulations. the annual report contains comments on the sixth, seventh and eighth european development funds. these are currently separated and accompanied by a separate declaration. the audit revealed some problems with respect to the edf regulations, as well as errors in the amount of payments made. apart from these points, the court of auditors nevertheless considers that the accounts of the european development fund are reliable and that the transactions relating to them are legal and regular. in these circumstances, in most areas of expenditure, the court of auditors has identified poorly defined policies and programmes which cannot be properly evaluated, making it impossible to estimate precisely the resources needed. the results are therefore not very convincing and the result is a waste of funds. in our special report no 2/99 on the impact of the reform of the community's agricultural policy on the cereals sector, the court of auditors noted that there is no evidence that the reduction in institutional prices has benefited consumers to any great extent or that the reform has improved the conditions of small farmers. policies and programmes lack clear and measurable objectives in terms of costs and returns, so it is impossible to see how much the desired objectives have been achieved and whether the money has been spent. the main indicator used to measure financial performance is the extent to which the appropriations allocated under the budget have been used and not the efficiency with which they have been spent. this confirms the persistence of the spending culture within the community, which is much more concerned with the volume of expenditure than with its quality. i would stress that these remarks concern the community as a whole. at the same time, evaluations are not conducted in a consistent manner and rarely lead to concrete corrective action. this is the case, for example, with medium-term evaluations of structural measures: the methodological framework remains inadequate and we lack appropriate indicators. the commission must ensure that a proper link is established between the results of evaluations and programming. the 1998 annual report again reveals weaknesses in the three levels of community financial control: the commission, the member states' systems, and the commission's supervision of these systems. the commission's internal control has not prevented the problems of mismanagement and irregularities which have recently been brought to light. at the same time, several bodies are responsible for internal audit, which shows a lack of coordination. the court's audit of the 1998 accounts revealed cases where weaknesses in internal control led to ineligible costs being financed by the commission, excessive payments, outdated contracts or a lack of supporting documents. these factors affected the court of auditors' statement of assurance, particularly in the field of internal policies. we cannot rely on the control systems of the member states to prevent errors.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, what seems extremely technical in your announcement is in fact a significant improvement in the protection of victims of road accidents in a different country. i say this because we are apparently no longer able to talk to people in a way that they understand what it is about. we can be proud of this directive. this is a joint effort by the european parliament, which took the initiative, and the commission, which significantly improved on the original parliament proposal by introducing the compensation body. but we can also thank the council for accepting the proposal in its basic points. as regards the recommendations for second reading, i would like to focus on two points. most of the amendments concern wording, the legal text itself. the council's common position contains passages which are simply incomprehensible. i'm even convinced that the authors don't know what they're writing. i would like to remind the commission and the council of a very fine phrase of a german jurist from the last century. he said that the legislator should think like a philosopher and speak like a farmer, simply and clearly, so that everyone can understand. the art of compromise often has consequences for legislation, which can no longer respect the principle of simplicity and clarity. however, there is one specific problem on which the european parliament does not share the view of the commission and the council. i would remind the commission and the council that we have the support of practice on this point, the support of the insurers in question - which is also true of the whole of the directive. we also have the support of the automobile industry, we have the support of the associations of accident victims. only the commission and the council are not yet in favour of this. what is it ? this directive should also apply when the accident does not take place in an eu member state but in a third country. there is absolutely no reason not to apply the directive in this case. let's say a frenchman and an italian get into an accident in switzerland. why should the directive not apply in this case? why would you do that ? the insurers shake their heads and say there's no problem. only one british insurance company disagrees. but all the other girls say , " why not ? " with this directive we are not changing anything at all in the law, we are not changing anything in the courts, we are not changing anything in the legal procedures. the only difference is that in the example above, the french victim does not have to go directly to the italian insurance company in italy, but to the representatives of the italian insurance company in france. this is the case regardless of the third country where the accident occurred, here in switzerland. this directive does not change anything about the other procedures, in case the parties do not agree. it merely improves the pre-litigation settlement of the dispute, not the judicial settlement. that is why i ask you, commissioner. there were obviously vested interests at stake. the commission even stated in a trilogue that european insurers would be against my solution. that is not true, they are in favour of this solution. i therefore recommend, commissioner, that the commission should review its position. she's not defendable. i assume that the council will also accept this solution if necessary. i would like to stress once again that this proposal was not conceived on paper. this proposal was the result of countless discussions with all parties involved. that is why i believe it is useful, because those who have experienced it in practice say that it works, it works wonderfully well, and that is what we want too. normally, the commission will hear the parties concerned. so ask the circles concerned and you will find that they approve the solution proposed by the european parliament. there is therefore no reason to limit the application of the directive. it would only harm the victims. we must not forget it ! we want to improve the protection of victims of accidents. i therefore urge that we all think about this matter once again in the pending conciliation procedure.

the finnish presidency of the council is now leaving us because the finns are also expected to make a new appointment of their member already present at the court of auditors. under article 247 (3) of the treaty establishing the european community and the corresponding provisions of the ecsc and euratom treaties, parliament must give its opinion on the nominees before the council, acting unanimously, appoints the members of the court of auditors for a renewable term of six years. by letter of 3 november 1999, the council invited the parliament to deliver its opinion and sent it the names and curricula vitae of the candidates. the council was to consider the appointment of mr reynders (belgium), mr fabra vallés (spain), mrs geoghegan-quinn (ireland) and mr caldeira (portugal) and the confirmation of mr mohr (denmark), mr salmi (finland), mr clemente (italy) and mr karlsson (sweden). as provided for in rule 35 of our rules of procedure, the committee on budgetary control heard and questioned the proposed candidates separately on 22 and 23 november 1999. in doing so, we have first of all been guided by the provisions of the treaty. these require that candidates belong or have belonged to external audit institutions or have a special qualification for this function. in any case, their independence is the main requirement. in addition, we have included in our deliberations the guidelines of the two parliamentary resolutions of 1992 and 1995 by mr lamassoure and mr bourlanges. i can tell you that after careful consideration the committee on budgetary control has concluded that the candidates meet the criteria for appointment to the court of auditors and has given a favourable opinion on each of the eight candidates. we are particularly pleased that, if parliament agrees to this report, two women will sit on the court of auditors' fifteen-member panel. i would remind you that at the time of the last appointment we made it a condition for parliament's assent that at least one woman should be among the candidates to be appointed. we had one female candidate at the time, another came along. i think we're making some progress. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. these are the rules governing the procedure. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. we discussed the court of auditors' report for 1998 on monday. some very important tasks have been set out for us to carry out. i am thinking first of all of the fact that the court's report clearly states, and i can only emphasize this, that we must change the culture of spending. the court of auditors has given some very important indicators in this respect. given that we have just discussed the 2000 budget in depth and that parliament wanted to move towards multiannual planning of funding in crisis regions, such as the balkans for example, this is a perspective towards which we must orientate ourselves more than to disperse into small isolated programmes or projects, which do not allow for effective control and require greater personnel expenditure than the real objectives that should be achieved. for us, it's about working with goals, not expenses. that is why i have no difficulty in agreeing with the court of auditors: we need better financial management. we already have - at least in part - proposals from the commission on how this should be done. however, parliament must also give a very thorough opinion on the matter. we can no longer afford to see a large number of citizens of the european union saying no to europe. we must all work on this, listen to the proposals drawn up by the court of auditors and incorporate them into our analyses in order to get a positive response from the peoples of europe once again to what unites us.

climate change decided to establish a two-year work programme, the buenos aires action plan. the programme should lead to decisions on the issues not resolved by the kyoto protocol being taken by the sixth conference of the parties (cop 6) to be held in the hague in one year's time. in this context, the expectations expressed in bonn focused on the need for substantial technical changes. it was clear from the outset that important political decisions would have to wait for the sixth conference of the parties. i think that step forward has been made. one element of cop 5 was of enormous political importance: chancellor schröder's request that the protocol should be in force by 2002. i am glad that the european union, as well as many other parties, have supported this idea. this implies that a precise timetable is now in place, one that increases the pressure on all parties to make cop 6 a success. i call on all parties to ensure that the ratification process can be launched immediately after cop 6. against this background, the decision taken by the parties in bonn to accelerate the process in the coming years is important. let me make a few remarks on some of the issues that were discussed in bonn. the most important issues not resolved by the kyoto protocol concern the rules and modalities for the kyoto mechanisms and the design of a global flexible system. the kyoto mechanisms - emissions trading, joint implementation and clean development mechanism - are part of the protocol. it is generally recognised that these mechanisms are able to ensure a good cost-effectiveness of climate action. it is of course crucial that this system is accompanied by a system of absolute compliance with provisions for cases of non-compliance. in view of the difficulty of the international negotiation process, it is very positive that we have de facto reached draft negotiating texts on the kyoto mechanisms and compliance. these texts will remain the basis for further negotiations in the coming months. without this, we would have had little chance of reaching decisions at cop 6. significant progress has also been made on capacity building, technology transfer and adaptation to the effects of climate change. the meeting again highlighted the importance of making equal progress on issues of interest to the industrialized world as well as on issues of interest to developing countries. that is why we need a balanced process between the issues of the kyoto protocol and the underlying issues of the climate change convention. let us not forget that if we are to guarantee the success of cop 6, we must achieve significant results on both these issues, by building a bridge between the industrialized and the developing countries. another success was the continuation of the so-called joint activities. these projects funded by the industrialised countries can only improve capacity building and technology transfer in developing countries and economies in transition. this brings me to a very important issue which was also raised by parliament in a resolution: the choice of nuclear energy as an option for clean development mechanism projects. i believe that the environmental and safety problems of nuclear energy are too great to encourage its proliferation in developing countries under the label of a clean development mechanism. there are excellent alternatives such as renewable energy sources and energy efficiency measures, which are much more in line with the clean development mechanism's objectives of encouraging sustainable development. i shall now deal with some of the points of divergence. the eu's proposal for a concrete ceiling for the use of the kyoto mechanisms was not formally addressed at cop 5, but it was the subject of extensive discussions in the corridors. the intentions behind these proposals are stronger than ever and ensure that all parties can meet, at least to a large extent, their own emission targets at home rather than relying heavily on the kyoto mechanisms. this should allow the first behavioural and technological changes to be made in preparation for the much more ambitious emission reductions we will experience in the future. moreover, the kyoto targets must be achieved through real emission reductions and not by buying the 'right to pollute' from another country. these rights have become far too generous because of the economic downturn - the famous "hot air" licensing trade. hence the need to limit the amount of emissions that one country can sell to another. cop 6 will have to decide how to ensure that these environmental protection measures are integrated into the overall package of decisions. the community's position on ceiling issues has not changed. another important element of cop 5 was the voluntary commitments made by developing countries in this area. we welcome the fact that developing countries such as argentina and kazakhstan are deliberately choosing to reduce their own greenhouse gas emissions. their participation in international climate change action is of paramount importance for the economic growth prospects of these countries. reductions. i hope to be able to stand before you in about a year's time to share with you the positive results of cop 6. in the meantime, the commission will not only continue to take an active part reduce the cost to our economies of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. we still have a lot of work to do on the technical and political level if we are to implement the kyoto protocol, which would be a first step in the fight against global warming. i appreciate your commitment to spreading the importance of fighting climate change in europe and to your counterparts in other countries, especially in the us congress.

commission - (el) mr president, my reply will be in two parts: firstly, i will refer to what has been achieved so far since the beijing conference and how the european union has supported the actions adopted in the relevant platform, and then i will address the role of the european parliament in preparation for the special session of the united nations to be held in the summer of 2000. i agree with mrs theorin that the situation of women is dramatic in many parts of the world and is even deteriorating. unfortunately, globalisation, development, technology and the free movement of capital, goods and especially people have often had a negative impact on women and children in the third world. i will mention some of the actions undertaken by the commission, but i would like to stress that in my view there is still a very large scope for new initiatives, both in the commission and in the member states, and that it is naturally necessary to pursue a specific policy of support for these issues, as was done during the preparations for beijing and subsequently in the context of the fifth action plan. as is well known, in 1995, in parallel with the beijing conference, the commission issued a communication which provided for the integration of the gender dimension into all development policies. in 1995, a resolution was adopted to integrate this dimension into all relevant policies and the guidelines for the commission services to take into account were set out. a budget line has been set aside for awareness-raising and support for women's actions in developing countries. an agreement was reached on the development of indicators and in april 1999 the first communication on results was published for common indicators to take account of the situation of women in the economic, political and social spheres, taking into account the development programmes adopted; finally, in 2000, the first biennial report will be published, assessing the results of these policies. i repeat that some actions have been taken after beijing, but they must be stepped up and we must move towards more concrete measures. as regards the contribution of the european parliament, it must be acknowledged that for years it has played a leading role in raising awareness among european and international opinion, but also in the decision-making process, since it has a bearing on the measures taken by the council and the commission. parliament therefore has a decisive role to play, and the effects of this will be particularly felt throughout the preparations for the special session in june. you know that there is a committee on preparatory questions in which parliament participates. the member states participate in the organisation of the united nations session. as the presidency has stressed, we will be taking part as observers. we have gained experience from the beijing conference, but this will not prevent us from having permanent and practical cooperation throughout this preparatory period in order to reach common positions among the fifteen, which is of vital importance in order to give them more weight and to make them more effective in june.
