commission. - (el) madam president, i would like to thank all the members who took part in this debate. there is no denying that the beijing conference was a major event, as we see every year. and i think that when the first review takes place in june, beyond the unfortunate findings that are emerging again from the statistics, figures and data on the situation of women in the world, we will also note some encouraging developments. i shall try to answer all questions as specifically as possible. following the adoption of the beijing platform for action and the commitment of the 189 countries concerned, the european union and our region have taken action at three levels: firstly, at the level of the member states, secondly, at the level of the union's political strategy, and thirdly, at the level of the union's policy towards developing countries. and on these three levels, which are equally important, there is already a balance sheet and the programme of future activities will be submitted shortly. i would like to stress, however, as the speakers have done, that the member states and governments have the primary responsibility for fulfilling the commitments of the beijing platform. the european union is involved at the second level with a view to a horizontal strategy. what are we doing and what are the procedures? three events are to be held before the june special session: the economic committee meeting in january, the european conference on the follow-up to beijing in february and the meeting of the united nations commission on the status of women in march. we shall have to make an effort to coordinate these events so that our contribution to the june session is effective. firstly, as regards the regional conference, it is very important to achieve concrete results which will be the subject of general agreement at the end of the debate and which we will take into account when we meet again at the european conference in february. who will be in the final ? first of all, of course, the european parliament, then the non-governmental organisations and, in this connection, as the question has been raised, i would say that the women's movement and the ngos have played and are playing a key role in being the real driving forces in policy-making at european level. finally, of course, the commission with many of its departments, the member states and the presidency will also be involved. during the preparatory phase - you know there is a committee, which i have already mentioned - the 12 areas of concern identified in beijing will be discussed. i will respond to a comment by mrs theorin that we are not in a position at this stage to give priority to four or five areas, because the beijing platform commits us to giving equal priority to the 12 areas, but it goes without saying that when we debate the fifth action programme we can focus on setting priorities at european level. these 12 areas of concern will be examined by the following groups under the mainstreaming headings: the gender dimension in development policy, i.e. the situation of gender equality in all european union cooperation activities with developing countries, women's participation and human rights. these groups will be associated horizontally and vertically with beijing's 12 areas of concern. it is of the utmost importance that we reach consistent results and a common position which will be that of the european union at the special session in june. as some parallels have been made with the seattle meeting, i would point out that the institutional framework is not the same and that the commission does not have the same role in new york as it did in seattle at the beijing conference, but there is nothing to prevent the presidency, the commission and parliament - if there is the political will - from cooperating throughout the six months between now and june in order to join forces, and i am fully committed to the commission, which will ensure both continuous information and infrastructural support for parliament's proposals and work until the last day. i think that by june we will be able to find the final formula, which, as you know, is not based on a decision by the commission - or even by the council - since it is a matter for the united nations, where participation is at the level of the states, but, i repeat, there is the political will and the necessary conditions, since on many issues there is a complete identity of views which enables us to go forward together. i would like to conclude with another observation: movements, political initiatives and campaigns can often play a decisive role. i'll focus on the women's committee's latest initiative for a campaign against violence. it should be noted that a simple initiatives of this kind at world level, since these are issues you have already raised.
commission. - i would first like to apologize to my colleague, mr david byrne. unfortunately, due to the cancellation of this morning's brussels-strasbourg flight due to exceptionally bad weather conditions, he is unable to be here in person. i will therefore be the one to speak to you on this important subject, the measures taken by the commission in response to france's repeated refusal to lift its embargo on british beef. commissioner byrne will, however, arrive in strasbourg later this afternoon. the commission will then be able to hear all your questions when it adopts the proposal for a regulation on the labelling of bovine products. he will also be pleased to meet with individual members of parliament or groups of members to discuss the matter in greater depth. in these circumstances, which could not be avoided, i can only communicate to you, on his behalf, the text of mr byrne. as you know, yesterday the commission decided to issue a formal reasoned opinion to the french authorities in view of their continued refusal to lift their national restrictions on imports of british beef. the french authorities have five working days to reply to this letter. if france refuses to lift its embargo, the case will be brought before the european court of justice. we have not been able to resolve this matter amicably. the commission is very disappointed. it is fair to say that all parties involved are also very disappointed, given the enormous efforts made to find a solution to the problem without resorting to legal action. the commission has always made it very clear that it prefers to resolve this conflict without going through the legal channels. this approach is in the interest of all parties. i would add that it is mainly for the benefit of the most affected parties, namely the british beef producers. one thing is certain: legal action to lift the embargo will probably take a long time and is a second choice to a friendly solution. the commission's efforts have been concentrated on one point: establishing that the original decision to lift the embargo on british beef was not a threat to public health. this decision was based on a series of important safeguards which were strongly supported by scientific advice. the commission also followed the guidelines of the florence european council of june 1996 on the procedures, timetable and safeguards required to lift the embargo. unfortunately, the french authorities, on the advice of their french food safety agency, afssa, were still not prepared to lift their national restrictions. the commission took the precaution of referring these questions to its scientific steering committee in order to obtain its opinion and to find out whether it had any doubts about the decision to lift the embargo and, in particular, the timing of the date-based export regime. the scientific steering committee gave a unanimous and largely reassuring opinion on this point: there is no need to review the decision on the lifting of the embargo on british beef exports. unfortunately, this was not enough to convince the french authorities to lift the embargo. efforts were then made to provide further guarantees and further clarifications on the provisions relating to the date-based export regime. these efforts enabled the united kingdom, france and the commission to agree on a memorandum of understanding on 23 november last, which contained all the necessary guarantees and clarifications. we honestly thought that this protocol would allow the french embargo to be lifted. however, the opinion of afssa on this protocol was not sufficient to decide that the french authorities should lift the embargo. on 9 december they formally informed the commission of their decision. the commission therefore adopted a reasoned opinion yesterday. some have criticised the commission's efforts to resolve this conflict diplomatically as a waste of time and energy. in fact, they would have preferred the commission to take legal action directly. these criticisms are unfounded. they're dangerous, too. as i have already pointed out, they are contrary to the interests of the most affected party, the british beef producers. these criticisms also overlook the very determined measures taken by the commission to comply with its obligations under the treaty and to ensure that community law is respected. in fact, the commission played the carrot (the intensive efforts to bring the parties together and reach an agreement through negotiations) and the stick (the measures to be taken when the efforts clearly were not sufficient). it should be borne in mind that the letter of formal notice filed on 16 november allowed only a two-week period for reply, not the usual two months. the reasoned opinion adopted by the commission yesterday also provides for a time limit of five days instead of two months. in fact, this has not caused any delay in the legal timetable to be implemented to comply with the decision to lift the embargo on british beef exports. the interim period served to provide much needed guarantees to demonstrate that the decision to lift the embargo was indeed justified. in particular, it established the validity of the scientific basis on which the decision to lift the embargo was based. i am sure that if this conflict is ever resolved amicably, and i hope it can still be, it will be thanks to the efforts we have made in the last few weeks. thank you for your attention. let me again apologize to commissioner byrne who is not here in person. he'll be here to answer your questions later, though.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, commissioner, the ban on the marketing and administration of bst expires at the end of 1999. so this matter has become urgent for us. the commission proposal aims to ban the placing on the market and administration of bst to dairy cows. the commission is based on scientific studies which confirm that the administration of bst to animals causes avoidable pain. therefore, as stated in the report, i reject, in the name of animal welfare, the placing on the market and use of bst in the european union. i would remind you that all the member states have approved and ratified the european convention for the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. the use of bst increases the risk of nipple and foot lesions and has a negative influence on reproduction. there are also reports of loss of profitability, premature disposal of animals unsuitable for breeding and deaths. the numbers speak for themselves. bst increases the risk of mastitis by 25%, infertility by 18%, and paralysis by 50%. but the arguments against the use and marketing of bst are not limited to animal welfare, but also include health and economic considerations. bst is also rejected by consumers. it is therefore easy to imagine that if bst were to be used, consumers would change their habits, which would increase the imbalance in the dairy, milk products and beef sectors. what is even more absurd is that we are already producing surpluses in normal times. bst is not a therapeutic product and is only used to increase milk production. the milk quota system was introduced precisely to reduce milk production and with the bst we would make a mockery of that system. that can't be the case. exports would also suffer. with the exception of the united states, no major purchaser or producer of milk and milk products worldwide authorizes the use of hormones. we were elected as representatives of the citizens and therefore of the consumers. we should therefore take our mission seriously and look after the interests of the electorate. bst is a hormone produced by genetic engineering. so far, no member state has carried out field trials with regard to bst. the changes in the composition of milk which bst can cause have not been definitively established and it is not even possible to assess the effects of genetic engineering on human health. the fact that only a few countries have authorized the use of this hormone cannot lead to a weakening of international health standards. but more decisively, consumers are rejecting bst. it is no coincidence that large supermarket chains declared as early as 1994 that, following a consumer survey, they would under no circumstances sell milk from bst-treated cows, even if the eu moratorium was lifted. what we cannot explain to the consumer, however, is that already today several eu member states import dairy products containing bst - many of them from the usa, the czech republic, slovakia and bulgaria - and that these products have therefore long been on our consumers' plates, such as cheeses made from this type of milk. since third countries authorizing the use of this hormone are not required to make an official announcement, the commission does not currently have an exhaustive list of these countries. i think that is an appeal that should be made to the commission again. the commission should first examine whether bst is harmful to human health and secondly what possibilities there are to make imports of bst products truly transparent. the commission proposal does not address the production of bst in member states or the import of this substance as long as it is intended for export to third countries. in conclusion, let me say this: we all have a hard time explaining to our electorate that bst is already produced in some member states but cannot be used here. i do not know whether, in the context of job preservation alone, we should not also be critical about this. we are in agreement with the commission and i hope that we can approve this urgent measure and close this matter tomorrow. i thank all those who have participated in this work. - (de) mr president, one of our colleagues has just said that the compulsory beef labelling system will not be introduced until 1 january 2001. i can inform you that the council has apparently accepted our request to bring forward the date of introduction of this system to 1 september 2000. this decision represents a small victory for parliament, at least in terms of the time limit. however, the council did not make this commitment in the codecision procedure. if that were the case, it would have had to approve, by a simplified procedure, all the other amendments we voted for yesterday in this house. in the case of a codecision procedure, everything would have been up to us. instead, the council acted under the old regulation 820/97 in accordance with article 19 of the implementing provisions. it decided that states still had the possibility of extending the voluntary labelling system until 1 september 2000. i don't think that's very fair either. this decision, however, is a reconciliation with the position of the european parliament. apart from that, we are now in a codecision procedure with regard to the other amendments we voted for yesterday, which brings us back to 1 january 2000. the council must react to this. if he does not adopt our amendments, we will then find ourselves in the case of a consultation procedure. all the other matters we want to include in the regulation are still under discussion. i hope that we can also impose our views on the council and that the council will be able to be right.
(ppe-de), rapporteur. - mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. - (de) mr president, commissioner, five minutes on a friday is enough. i have prepared for a shorter speaking time, but this will allow me to add a few remarks without going overboard. hop is a special plant. (applause) it is this that ultimately gives flavour and bitterness to this most precious of popular foods: beer. (applause) the truth lies not only in wine, but also in beer. this is particularly important for bavaria, the land of my birth, where this product, this commodity, has played an important role both in terms of historical development and employment. white beer is obviously a very special variety of beer; she's well known in munich and is liked by many people. hops could grow quickly anywhere, but it is also up to very special individuals to provide the necessary care, so that hops can be grown successfully. there are also some interesting sayings on this subject: "like a twig and a tater-toe, so is a hop". in essence, this means that hops are a rather capricious fruit that rewards those who devote all their attention to it, but punishes those who neglect the work. another saying is: "the hops need a daily master". in short, hops are a fruit that requires a lot of work and will only thrive in the hands of the hardworking man. the area devoted to hop growing in our country has therefore been constantly increasing. in the heart of bavaria, in hallertau, a large hop growing area has been developing for over 150 years. it is in fact the largest hop region in the world, with a quarter of production coming from hallertau. you will understand why this subject is so dear to bavaria and to me as a bavarian. (applause) i would like to thank i would like to stress again that hops and hop beer evoke comfort and relaxation somewhere. hops also have medicinal properties. bavaria is known above all as the land of beer, but also as a region of tradition and progress. you have probably heard that tradition and progress are of particular importance in bavaria. the expression "leather panties and laptop" is also frequently used by the bavarian minister-president edmund stoiber. the bavarian region is not only famous for the annual oktoberfest in munich, but also for its high-tech industry. it is not for nothing that the world-renowned university of brewing engineering münchen-weihenstephan is also located in bavaria. from here, knowledge was exported around the world, particularly to china, russia and the united states, where it had a considerable influence on hop growing and beer production. that is why the saying is often heard: "god himself wants his share of the dough". this is also important in relation to the regulation proposed by the commission. i would like to add a few remarks, but i must limit myself to the time allotted to me. i now come to the rules of procedure and the report. the main purpose of this is to delete certain articles which have become obsolete because of the expiry of the time limits and the content of the common organisation of the market in hops. the detailed report will therefore no longer have to be submitted once a year but once every five years, since the council has fixed a flat-rate aid for a period of five years. i think this is a good idea, madam commissioner, with one objection. the experience gained by bavaria in this field is undoubtedly what is urging us to be more cautious. that is why i propose that data on the evolution of the area under cultivation, demand, variety distribution, price and crop trends in each member state should continue to be collected annually and made available to operators each year. i have obtained a promise from the commission that this data will be made available on the internet. that is why i have tabled two amendments. i ask parliament to approve them. i know, however, that the commission does not view these two amendments very favourably. but parliament is not really the commission. i therefore call for these amendments to be adopted. (laughter and applause)

commission. - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr xaver mayer, for his valuable work - and perhaps especially for his enthusiastic presentation of the hops paradise of bavaria. i also thank the committee on agriculture and rural development for its constructive attitude. i am glad that our proposal to reorganise the hop market has been well received. the commission proposal is designed to remove provisions which are no longer valid either because the time limits for their application have expired or because of previous changes in our common organization of the market in hops. these amendments must be made before the basic provision is consolidated. since the council has decided that the level of aid will be constant for five years, the commission does not consider it necessary to produce an annual report on the situation of hop production and sales. the commission therefore considers that article 11 can be deleted. however, under article 18, we will present a thorough assessment of this situation by 1 september 2000. i am therefore afraid that the two amendments proposed by parliament will unnecessarily complicate the text, and i think that the requirement for annual information is already covered by the new proposal. this information will also be available on the internet. in these circumstances, the commission has every reason to reject these two amendments.

- (de) mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, tajikistan is not only the poorest of the former soviet states, it is also the one which has suffered the most during the last five years from the chaos caused by tribal strife, before it finally degenerated into civil war. the country did not understand that it had to use the financial assistance granted so far for the intended purpose. only in recent months has there been a return to some calm, after the belligerents suspended hostilities and decided to form a coalition government in the near future. parliamentary elections are scheduled for march 2000. international donors, including swiss organizations, are again ready to provide this financial aid under certain conditions. after the calm has returned and the development prospects have become relatively more favourable, the savary report now tries to give the country the financial aid in question again in the form of a loan. with this measure, we hope that tajikistan will receive a clear signal to improve the organisation of the state in the direction of democratic development and to undertake the necessary reforms. however, this financial assistance in the form of a loan should be granted only under several conditions: that the european union can effectively carry out a proper control of the financial assistance, that the process of national reconciliation continues and that the elections, and especially the legislative elections in march 2000, are organised in a free and democratic manner. as mr savary has very rightly pointed out, this is also the aim of amendments nos 8 and 9, which seem to us to be quite explicit. if tajikistan's solvency and soundness were to be restored, this proposal in the 2000 budget should also be welcomed. the rapporteur, mr bourlanges, has just confirmed to me that a commentary should be included to the report, stating that financial aid can again be granted in some form under the tacis programme. in conclusion, let me add that the epp-ed group supports this report, despite all the risks involved. this is a new and potentially successful attempt to relaunch and encourage economic and technical cooperation with tajikistan.
- (de) mr president, if the tajik people did not exist, i would not be standing before you today. during world war i, my grandfather was taken prisoner and sent to what was then russian central asia to build railroads. he always told me that he was able to survive those difficult years only because of the hospitality and helpfulness of the tajik people. but that is not why i am investing so much in tajikistan today. because, unlike my colleague mr blokland, i think this is a matter of direct concern to us. tajikistan is located in a territorial space bounded by china and russia, which meet here, as well as the islamic world and the caspian sea, where there are huge deposits of raw materials. i believe that we are dealing here with a balkan of the future, a balkan on a global scale. it is therefore in our interest to stabilise the region and prevent ethnic conflicts from spreading to the rest of the world, especially when we know that a number of nuclear powers live there. that is why i think it is necessary to help tajikistan to take this perilous path by granting a loan, but also by granting loans which are likely not to be repaid, while knowing full well that we will have to turn to the member states, since our budget does not allow us to do so. we should of course demand the development of democracy and the rule of law, but we must avoid imposing inappropriate revenue on them. for centuries, tajikistan's wealth was plundered by colonial powers. it was under communist rule for 80 years. today, this small mountain people is trying to find its way and we cannot impose european recipes on them. we must advocate measures comparable to those adopted in relation to developing countries, including african countries, where many things are still highly questionable, but which we have been helping for decades to find the way to democracy. tajikistan has only been receiving our aid for a few years. we must therefore demand that certain rules be observed, while at the same time showing patience towards the tajik people. we should therefore massively encourage the elections to be held in the spring and recognize that this is not only an event that is a credit to europe, but that it is also in europe's very special interest to contribute to the emergence of peace in this region.
